maintopic: CANADIAN ARMY
CANADIAN ARMY
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP LIEUTENANT-GENERAL H. D. G. CRERAR TO COMMAND FIRST CANADIAN ARMY

speechtext:
On the order of motions:
lion. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence): Mr. Speaker, I have an announcement with regard to the army which I consider sufficiently important to make at this time. I have to inform the house that Lieutenant-General H. D. G. Crerar, CD., D.S.O., has been appointed to command the First Canadian Army. General Crerar took over this morning from Lieutenant-General Kenneth Stuart, C.B., D.S.O., M.C. Lieutenant-General Stuart is chief of staff at Canadian military headquarters, and has also been holding temporarily the post, of army commander, in which he has given exceptionally fine service. General Stuart will continue in his substantive post as chief of staff at Canadian military headquarters. General Crerar, along with his own wide experience and his high qualities as a soldier, becomes heir to the results of the labours of General McNaughton and the tens of thousands of officers and men who, like him, have worked unselfishly to bring the army organization to effective battle worthiness.
I have already placed on record in Hansard the recognition and deep appreciation of the government and the people of Canada, as expressed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself, of the outstanding service which General McNaughton has rendered to the army and to Canada as commander of the First Division, the Canadian Corps, and then the First Canadian Army.
I cabled General Crerar last night expressing every confidence in his leadership, and in the determination and fighting qualities of the army under his command. At the same time I sent to him and to them the heartfelt wishes of all Canadians for great success. I am sure that the house and the country will join very heartily in that expression of confidence and sincere good wishes.

Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, under the item for motions we find this paragraph:
Further consideration in committee of the whole of the report of the special committee on the revision of standing orders.
As this item constitutes an amendment to the statute of the House of Commons, will it be possible for the government to give sufficient notice to members to be present when this whole matter with regard to the rules of the house is discussed? At the last sitting the senior minister told us that the amendments to the rules may be taken up at any time. speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am as anxious as can be to meet the wishes of hon. members. But it is obviously quite impossible to attempt to satisfy everyone in the matter of the time at which certain measures may be taken up. As my hon. friend knows, members are expected to be in the house at all times. The government must proceed on that basis. Notice is given in advance, where it is possible to do so, in order to further the convenience of hon. members. But that is wholly a matter of accommodation, so far as it can reasonably be carried out. There may be many occasions when this cannot be done. Beyond that I do not think the government should be expected to go in seeking to indicate the hour or day at which particular measures may be taken up.

speechtext:
Mr. ANGUS MacINNIS (Vancouver East) moved for leave to introduce bill No. 37, to amend the criminal code.
He said: This bill proposes an amendment to the criminal code by adding a new section, 318-A, to come after section 318, to prevent public utterances or the dissemination of material calculated or likely to cause discrimination or disharmony on account of race or religion. The utterance for publication of such statements tends to set race against race and religious groups against religious groups. speechtext: What actions were taken by the government with a view to providing additional workers in the coal mines?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: COAL PRODUCTION-MAN-POWER
speechtext:
(a)	Under arrangements between Department of National Defence and Department of Labour, coal miners receive special consideration for postponement of military service.
(b)	Personnel of armed services in Canada with coal mining expeiience are granted leave of absence (without pay and allowances) if willing to return to the coal mines; in certain instances they are granted discharge from the armed forces. (Such personnel are encouraged by both national defence and selective service officers to return to the coal mines).
(c)	Under instructions of national selective service, permits are not issued for coal miners to seek any other employment.
(d)	Order in council P.C. 4092 issued in May 1943 requires ex-coal mine workers to return to the mines regardless of present civilian occupations. They are guaranteed full employment.
(e)	Orders in council P.C. 4861, June 17, 1943 and P.C. 6077, July 29, 1943 give national selective service officers authority to direct any male person over 16 years and less than 65 years of age, to accept and enter specified employment in coal mining.
(f)	Order in council P.C. 121, January 1944, provides that no person engaged as a coal mine worker will be accepted prior to August 1, 1944 for enlistment in any branch of the armed services, except under permit issued by a national selective service officer.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CANADIAN ARMY
subtopic: CONDITIONS FOR GRANTING OF FARM SPRING LEAVE, 1944
speechtext:
Several members have made inquiries of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) with regard to the terms upon which farm spring leave is to be granted by his department. I wish now to make a statement with reference to the matter.
When informing the house last year of the terms upon which leave for this work was

Canadian Army-Spring Leave
being granted to army personnel, the minister suggested that the hopes of members of the house and of those engaged in fanning should not be raised too high.

maintopic: CANADIAN ARMY
subtopic: CONDITIONS FOR GRANTING OF FARM SPRING LEAVE, 1944
speechtext: He was quite right about that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CANADIAN ARMY
subtopic: CONDITIONS FOR GRANTING OF FARM SPRING LEAVE, 1944
speechtext:
In announcing the terms of farm leave for the present spring season, I repeat the minister's remarks, although, as I shall explain in a moment, leave this year is in some respects upon a more generous scale.
Following the conclusion of spring leave granted in 1943, an order (R.O. 3456) was issued providing for assistance to agriculture in two ways, (1) by granting compassionate farm leave to enable soldiers to return to their own or to the farm of their immediate family, where hardship would otherwise ensue, and (2) by detailing soldiers for farm duty in circumstances of emergency. It was decided to amend this order and to provide, in addition to the leave which may now be granted under it, for the granting of spring and harvest leave at appropriate seasons.
In the spring of 1943, seeding leave might be granted to, the following:
(a)	Personnel on strength of home war establishments of district depots, i.e., the members of the administrative and training staffs.
(b)	Other personnel on strength of district
depots, excluding those awaiting dispatch to basic training centres or awaiting allocation after completion of advanced or trades training.	.
(c)	Personnel of the Veterans Guard of Canada who had completed their training.
(d)	Personnel of operational units up to a limit of 5 per cent of the strength of such units and where the soldier applying had completed his individual training.
The order now provides that general service personnel who by age and pulhems profile are suitable for overseas service will not be eligible for spring leave.
Subject to this exception, spring leave may be granted not only to those on strength of the home war establishments of district depots, but also to those on the home war establishment of any unit. Other personnel on the strength of district depots, except those awaiting dispatch to training centres or schools, will be eligible, as well as will also personnel of the Veterans Guard of Canada
and personnel on strength of operational units, as was the case last year, but the restriction to five per cent of those on strength of operational units to whom leave may be granted has been removed.
The period for which leave may be granted has been increased from six weeks to two months.
As was the case in 1943, applications for spring leave will be submitted by the soldier to his commanding officer and by him, in turn, to the general or district officer commanding concerned, who has been authorized to grant the leave in appropriate cases. It should, however, be distinctly understood that the leave to be granted under this order, as in every other type of leave, is subject to the exigencies of the service and can be granted by general or district officers commanding only if, in their opinion, essential army activities will not be substantially interfered with.
I have indicated that routine order No. 3456 has been amended in order to set out the terms upon which farm spring leave for 1944 is to be granted. I have here an office consolidation of the order with all amendments to date and, in order that hon. members interested may have available in convenient form information with regard not only to the granting of spring leave, harvest leave, and compassionate farm leave but also information as to the circumstances in which soldiers may be required to perform farm duty, I would ask leave of the house to table order No. 3456 as amended and to have it printed in Votes and Proceedings.

maintopic: APPLICABLE TO ACTIVE FORMATIONS, UNITS, AND PERSONNEL OF THE CANADIAN ARMY

speechtext:
Headquarters, Ottawa,
27th July, 1943.
3456-Compassionate Farm Leave, Spring Leave, Harvest Leave and Ordering Soldiers to Perform Farm Duty.
1.	This Order supersedes all previous orders and instructions dealing with the subject of army assistance to agriculture. This Order is effective as from 31st July, 1943, and will remain in effect until further notice.
2.	Seasonal conditions have created unusual difficulties in connection with agriculture. It is desired in cases of genuine merit that the army give such assistance as is possible consistent with army responsibilties.
3.	Such help as can be given is made much more effective if given promptly and it is, therefore, desired to make the procedure as simple and direct as possible. Heretofore, frequent references have had to be made to N.D.H.Q. in order to ensure uniformity of treatment across the country. It is felt, however, that the G.O's. C.-in-C. and the D.O's.C., being on the ground and having qow had good experience in connection with requests for agricultural help are in a position to appraise the circumstances.
4.	It has, therefore, been decided to put the matter in the hands of the G.O's. C.-in-C. and the D.O's.C., subject to certain necessary general principles. They are relied on to exercise sound judgment so as to help meet the immediate situation created by abnormal seasonal conditions whenever and wherever that can be done without substantial interference with essential army activities.
5.	Types of aid:
Assistance to agriculture will be given in the following ways:-
(a)	By granting of leave (known as Compassionate Farm Leave) to certain personnel under administrative provisions as outlined in Appendix "A" to this Order;
(b)	By the detailing for duty on farms (to be known as Farm Duty) of certain designated personnel under the authority of P.C. 5931, and under administrative provisions as outlined in Appendix "B" to this Order.
(c)	By granting of leave (known as Spring Leave or Harvest Leave, whichever may be applicable) to certain personnel under the administrative provisions outlined in the Appendix to this Order.
6 Principles Governing Grant of Aid:
There are certain principles which obtain in both the aforementioned cases:-
(a)	It is not possible to allow personnel to help in farm work if such action would, in the opinion of the G.O.C. or D.O.C.,

Canadian Army-Spring Leave
result in substantial intereference with essential army activities. The G.O's.C. and D.O's.C., should, however, endeavour to adjust and re-arrange personnel and duties so that such essential activities can be carried on for the period of the absence of personnel on farm work;
(b)	The farm must be a farm which contributes substantially to the national production over and above what is necessary for the occupants of the farm itself;
(c)	It is not possible at this time, which is1 the best training season of the year, to release men who are actually in training from Training Centres, except in special cases of compassionate grounds as mentioned in Appendix "A" hereto.
7.	Personnel Available:
Subject to the foregoing, the personnel from which assistance may be provided, are therefore:-
(a)	Personnel in disposal wings of Depots;
(b)	Personnel in home war establishments whom, by re-adjustment and re-arrangement, it may be possible to release for the time being. Regard shall be had to the continuing withdrawal of general service personnel for overseas duty;
(c)	Personnel in operational units also, having regard to the continuing withdrawal of general service personnel for overseas duty;
(d)	Personnel of the Veterans Guard of Canada.
8.	Personnel Not Available:
The following, although elegible for Compassionate Farm Leave, shall not be available for Spring Leave, Harvest Leave or Farm Duty:-
(a)	G.S. personnel who, by age and Pulhems Profile, are suitable for overseas service;
(b)	G.S. or N.R.M_A. personnel who are in training stream at Training Centres or Schools.
9.	Limitation as to number who may be granted Compassionate Farm Leave, Spring Leave, Harvest Leave and/or Detailed for Farm Duty.
Such numbers as G.O's.C. and D.O's.C. decide can be made available from any units in their command having regard to the exigencies of the service.
10.	G.O's.C.-in-C. and D.O's.C. will detail suitable members of their staffs to consult with the director, Dominion-provincial farm labour committee of the province concerned with a view of arranging to carry out the letter and spirit of this Order.
11.	The effective provisions of Order in Council, P.C. 5931 of 1943, are published for information as Appendix "D" to this Order.
(Effective 31st July, 1943.)
(H.Q. 54-27-55-4)
H.	F. G. LETSON,
Major-General.
Adjutant-General.
Appendix "A"

maintopic: COMPASSIONATE FARM LEAVE

speechtext:
1.	To Whom Granted:
This leave may be granted to men for the purpose of working on farms owned by members of their immediate family where there would be undue hardship if the leave were not granted. This leave is applicable where the relative working the farm is, because of old age or disability, incapable of continuing to do so and, by reason of their enlistment or enrolment, there is no other member of the family available to assist.
2.	Method of Application:
Application for Compassionate Farm Leave will be submitted in writing by the soldier to his Commanding Officer who will, after investigating, forward it, with his recommendation, to the G.O.C. or D.O.C. concerned. Such applications will not be referred to National Defence Headquarters. For the sake of uniformity, applications will be completed on M.F.M. 312 as amended to suit the circumstances.
3.	Duration and Renewal of Compassionate
Farm Leave:
The G.O.C. or D.O.C. may authorize leave for period applied for or such period as he deems advisable, but not to exceed six months. Subject to the exigencies of the Service, the same officers may grant extensions for such periods not exceeding six months as they may consider advisable.
4.	Investigation of Necessity for Leave:
The facilities of the N.S.S. Mob. Board, D.B.T., R.C.M.P., Auxiliary Services, or any Provincial, Municipal or Civic Organization may be used to investigate statements submitted on behalf of the applicant whenever the G.O.C. or D.O.C. considers it to be necessary or desirable.
5.	Transportation and Clothing:
The Department of National Defence will supply a suit of overalls and free transportation and meal tickets to all soldiers proceeding on Compassionate Farm Leave. Free return transportation shall be limited to destinations not more than 500 miles distant from the soldier's station and if the destination is more than 500 miles from the soldier's station, he shall furnish his own transportation jn excess of the 500 miles distance. The Department of Labour will pay the Department of National Defence the cost thereof on demand.
6.	Pay and Allowances:
Compassionate Farm Leave will be without pay of any kind or allowances of any kind, or subsistence, and soldiers will not be entitled to medical or dental attention, hospitalization, or compensation due to illness, injury or death while on Compassionate Farm Leave.
7.	Transfer to Depot in Certain Cases:
Personnel granted leave in excess of thirtyone days will be transferred to the District Depot of the Military District in which such leave is to be spent provided, however, that such transfer will be made effective the day following the commencement of leave. On such transfer the documents and other correspondence pertaining to the leave will be despatched
Canadian Army-Spring Leave

immediately to the appropriate District Depot, to which Depot the soldier will report on the expiration of his leave when he will be medically examined and if found fit, will be completed with clothing and equipment and will be either despatched with his documents to his former unit or otherwise disposed of by the District Officer Commanding.
8.	Clothing, Equipment, etc., on Proceeding on
Compassionate Farm Leave:
Where a soldier is granted leave up to but not exceeding 60 days under the provisions of this Order, he will be permitted to take with him necessary clothing and uniform. Except when specially authorized otherwise by the G.O.C. or D.O.C. concerned, he will only be authorized to wear his uniform while travelling to the place where he will reside during leave, and while returning from such place on the expiration of his leave. The cost of making good any deficiency in clothing or equipment issued to the man as shown on his M.F.C. 800, before proceeding on leave, or found to be deficient on his return from leave, will be recovered in the usual manner. Where leave for any period exceeding 60 days is granted, uniform and clothing will be worn only when authorized by the G.O.C. or D.O.C. When not so authorized, the man's uniform and clothing, and in all cases his equipment, will be returned to stores before the man proceeds on leave. The man will be responsible for providing any civilian clothing he may require when proceeding on leave.
9.	Furlough Form to be Furnished Soldier
Proceeding on Compassionate Farm Leave:
Before proceeding on leave the soldier will be given Furlough Form M.F.B. 322, with those portions of instructions on reverse side thereof which deal with dress and medical attention while on leave, struck out and initialled by the officer authorized to issue same. The 6oldier will be given explicit instructions in writing from his Officer Commanding which will include:
(a)	Conditions governing wearing of uniform;
(b)	Cessation of pay and allowances;
(c)	His being subject to recall at any time on 48 hours' notice;
(d)	His non-entitlement to dental and medical care during leave;
(e)	When and to whom, and how to apply if extension of leave required;
(f)	When, where, and to whom to report on expiration of leave required;
(g)	The necessity of obtaining his Commanding Officer's permission (under Routine Order No. 2242) to marry to be eligible for Dependents' Allowance on return from leave.
10.	Medical Examination of Soldier Proceeding on Compassionate Farm Leave:
If the period of leave exceeds 60 days, the soldier must be medically examined before proceeding on, and again after return from such leave. Should a soldier die, or be killed while on leave, either during or as a direct result of his employment but not otherwise, he will be entitled to a military funeral as a soldier in accordance with Article 220 of F.R. & I. (Canada).

He will also supply the soldier with a suit of overalls without charge to the soldier. The G.O.C. or D.O.C. will supply the said Director with information from time to time as to the names, units, etc., of personnel detailed for Farm Duty. The said Director will keep the G.O.C. or D.O.C. informed at all times as to the address of the soldier and with the name of the farmer on whose farm the soldier is performing Farm Duty.
3.	Priority of Employment:
Questions on priority of employment as between individuals or groups of individuals seeking to obtain soldiers for Farm Duty, as aforesaid, shall be settled by the Director, Dominion-Provincial Farm Labour Plan.

The personnel from which assistance may be
provided are:-
(a)	Personnel in disposal wings of Depots;
(b)	Personnel in Home War Establishments whom by readjustment and rearrangements, it may be possible to release for the time being. Regard shall be had to the continuing withdrawal of General Service personnel for overseas duty;
(c)	Personnel in Operational Units, also having regard to the continuing withdrawal of General Service personnel for overseas duty;
(d)	Personnel of the Veterans Guard of Canada.
5.	Who May Not be Detailed for Farm Duty:
The following, although eligible for Compassionate Farm Leave, shall not be available for Farm Duty:

Defence will supply free return transportation, meal tickets and a suit of overalls to all soldiers proceeding on Farm Duty, but the farmer will supply his board and lodging for the period of employment. Personnel detailed for Farm Duty shall .continue to be credited with their normal pay and allowances including trades pay and Dependents' Allowance, if payable, but not including subsistence allowance. It shall be the duty of the Director, Dominion-Provincial Farm Labour Plan, to keep regular time sheets on a pro-forma in quintup-licate to be supplied by the D.O.C. and at the expiration of the employment to obtain the signature of the farmer and the soldier certifying as to the accuracy of the time, rates, etc. These time sheets shall be certified as correct by the said Director and three copies shall be forwarded to the District Paymaster of the District to which the personnel belong, one copy being left with the farmer and the other copy being retained, by the Director. be made under arrangements to be formulated by the Department of Labour and are not to be collected by the soldier or by any other member of the Department of National Defence.

Personnel detailed for Farm Duty shall continue to be entitled to medical and dental treatment, hospitalization and all benefits on the same basis as though they were performing ordinary- military duty. On a point of order, Mr. Ohairman, I take it that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is about to commence a discussion with respect to the air services branch of the Department of Transport. Before that is done I Should like to make clear the position of the opposition as to the matter of procedure, and the sequence in which the departments are taken up under the war appropriation bill. I want to raise objection to what is being done, having in mind the statement of the government on Friday in connection with this matter. It was my understanding that the Department of Munitions and Supply would go on to-day, and I took it for granted that the minister would make his ordinary statement in connection with his department. As a matter of fact I think I am supported in that by the exchange which took place between the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). At the conclusion of the statement of the Minister of Munitions and Supply I find this, as reported at page 1587 of Hansard:
Mr. Stirling: The understanding was that this matter would be set aside to a future date so that it could be digested before the discussion continued.
The Prime Minister then indicated that that was a correct interpretation of the situation. Then when the business of the house was under discussion the whole question with respect to the ministry of munitions and supply was indicated as the procedure for to-day. Upon that basis our arrangements were made. To say the least I think it is unfair to ask us to go on with the discussion with respect to civil aviation, and I say that for one or two reasons which I believe will at once be understood and appreciated. First of all, this is the next sitting day after the day on which one of the major statements of the whole session was made. That statement involves one of the most important pieces of government policy so far announced. In addition to that, the report of Trans-Canada Air Lines was tabled to-day and referred to one of the committees of the house, but we have not yet seen it. Besides, we have now before us, for the first time, placed upon H-amard by the minister himself, the estimates for the air services branch of the Department of Transport.
I believe the committee will see clearly that to ask us to go on without any notice having been given is not fair. I would ask the government to review the position in order that at least there might be an opportunity to give closer study to one of the major matters being brought forward by the government. The Prime Minister will perhaps be the first to recognize the justice and wisdom of my suggestion. We do not ask for any lengthy period of time, because I do not think that would be proper. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I trust
j'ou will time me from this moment rather than from the moment I actually started, in view of the rather prolonged interruption. In this parliament we are dealing with a great many matters of extreme importance. Time will sort them out as to their relative significance. When that process has been completed I believe that the manner in which we deal with this question of air transport will loom large in the history of our time, it is only a few decades since the parliament of Canada was called upon to deal with matters pertaining to the rapid expansion of our railroad transportation facilities. I hope that we will avoid some of the mistakes that were made in those days and possess the imagination to sense what air transport will mean to civilization in Canada and throughout the world. I hope also that we will take the necessary steps to see to it that the full benefit of air transport is secured to the people of this country.
I should like to make a few remarks about the importance of air transport, dealing both 100-104
with the domestic and the international fields. Domestically it is obvious that travel by air is revolutionary, but there are some other things we should not lose sight of. Travel by air to the extent to which it is now possible will add tremendously to the sum total of the goods and services we shall be able to produce in this country. In a real sense air transport adds to the wealth of Canada. If we properly develop our facilities for air transport it should make possible greater travel on the part of our people between the various sections of our country, and should aid us in our desire to increase the knowledge of our people about Canada as a whole and develop our sense of nationhood and national unity.
Air transport properly developed should bring to remote areas in our country medical and hospital services and facilities of the kind which have been denied to the people in those areas. With a little imagination we should be able to realize that the full development of air transport may have an important bearing upon industry and upon the housing situation in this country. In due course air transport may make it possible to decentralize industry to an extent not hitherto possible. It introduces a new factor into the economic picture so far as industry is concerned. It is possible that a different civilization may grow up because of .this revolutionary development.
In this industrial age thus far it has been the practice to crowd people together in urban areas, with the resultant development of many bad features such as slum conditions and so on. We .recognize the desirability of people being able to spread out into rural areas and get more fresh air and sunshine, and I think we should let our imagination bring home to us the fact that the proper development of air transport may make possible better housing and living conditions for our people right across the country.
Another feature of our life which will be affected by the full development of air transport is life in the north country. Up to the present Canada has been thought of as strip of country running across the northern border of the country to the south. It is only in recent shears that we have begun to realize the potentialities of our north country, and I submit that the development of air travel will change those potentialities into realities.
On the international front it is recognized that this modern means of transport is of great importance. We can readily realize what air transport, if not properly controlled, may bring about in the way of unspeakable

War Appropriation-Transport

horrors in future wars. On the other hand, air transport, properly controlled, can aid in the establishment of permanent peace. On the one hand, it can do that by increasing the sum total of goods and services, increasing the wealth available in the world and in that positive way helping to bring about a better world in which war may not have to take place.
On the other hand, in attacking this problem of international air transport there is the possibility of developing cooperation among the nations. This cooperation can be built up in a functional way, as has already been referred to, as well as by the development of realistic organizations for the establishment and maintenance of world peace. I submit, therefore, that on every count this subject is one of great importance.
On behalf of the group with which I am associated I wish to say without hesitation that we welcome the statement made on Friday by the Minister of Munitions and Supply. I shall have some things to say about it in a few minutes which are critical, but in the main my criticism will be that it does not go far enough. Before making that criticism I want to say again that we welcome the statement and commend the government for 'having made known its position. I shall deal first with the international aspect of the statement.
May I first voice 1he hope that on this issue parliament will indicate that it stands behind the government as far as it has gone in preparing a draft international agreement. When the government sends its representatives to any international conference they should know that they can press for the implementation of everything in this proposed international convention. They should know that if everything therein is adopted it will be supported by any succeeding government. As I have already indicated, my point is that the draft convention should go further but to the extent it does go it should have the support of all groups in this house.
Having made the statement that in my view the proposed draft convention does not go far enough, it becomes my responsibility to indicate wherein I think it falls short. May I say first that when one approaches the whole problem of international control of air transport there are some basic matters that have to be agreed to. I feel that the minister stated those basic matters quite clearly, particularly when he referred to the necessity of agreeing to the right of innocent passage, and freedom of transit, and also his further statement with reference to freedom of com-
	!
mercial outlet within the limitations of certain regulations.
It might not be amiss to take a moment to look at the alternatives to international control of air transport. As I see it, there are two alternatives, and they are both extreme. On the one hand there is the possibility of what is miscalled the freedom of the air, the proposed right of companies anywhere and everywhere to fly anywhere and everywhere. I submit that if that were the case not only would we in Canada suffer materially but it would lead to all sorts of exploitation and rivalry and would be the basis for further disastrous wars. The other extreme from what I have said is miscalled the freedom of the air is the concept of narrow nationalism, the idea, for example, that each nation should set up boundaries around its own territory and refuse to allow planes in from other countries. One can see on that basis that we should soon be sidetracked in Canada. We should lose the advantage of our otherwise favourable position; and here too you will have not only the restricting of the people of the world with regard to the advantages of air transport but a development of ill-feeling and again a basis for international ill-will. Therefore I think we should recognize at the outset that either one of those extremes is out, and certainly should be out so far as Canada is concerned. Our representatives should go into any discussion on this question pledged to the idea of the international control of air transport.
As I see it, when one starts to discuss international control of air transport there are various matters that have to be considered. I see those matters falling on three different levels. On the first level there are such matters as safety regulations, rules of flying, standards of aircraft, standards of competency of the crews, ground equipment, meteorlogical services, navigational aids, and so on. On the second level are matters relating to the licensing of air routes, the arranging for quotas frequencies and rates, and also the whole concept of planning and fostering the development of various air routes in different parts ol the world. I pause for a moment to suggest that because one uses the word "licensing" in that connection it does not mean that the second level function is merely a restrictive function. I emphasize the fact that on this level initiative can be taken for the fostering and the developing of lines for the good of the whole world. But in addition to these two levels there is a third, namely, the level of operation of international air trunk routes, and seeing to it that the operation of such trunk routes will secure not to the owners of one

War Appropriation-Transport
company in one country but to the people of the world as a whole the full advantage of international air transport.
I think my criticism of the government's statement is obvious now that I have indicated these three levels. As I see the picture, the government has taken a fairly clear stand with respect to the matters which I say fall on the first and second levels. There are some details in the draft international air transport convention about which I shall make comments in a moment or two; but first of all I want to deal with the failure of the convention to refer to any of the matters which I have placed on the third level, namely, the level of international operation of international air transport. I should like to point out in that connection that my idea that this phase of the subject should be considered is not only ours but is contained in the statement which was issued by Australia and New Zealand on January 21, 1944. I should like to place on Hansard again one or two sections of the Australia-New Zealand agreement. Section 18 under civil aviation reads as follows:
18.	The two governments declare that the air services using the international air trunk routes should be operated by an international air transport authority.
19.	The two governments support the principles that
(a)	full control of the international air trunk routes and the ownership of all aircraft and ancillary equipment should be vested in the international air transport authority; and
(b)	the international air trunk routes should themselves be specified in the international agreement referred to in the next succeeding clause.
The point I wish to make in urging that this other phase of the subject should be considered is that I do not altogether agree with the statement of the minister, or with the parts that express the same thought in paragraph 3 of the summary or in article X, section 4 of the proposed convention, that it is of no concern to us who owns the lines from other countries which are participating in international air services. My contention is that if you have large private corporations from other countries participating in those international air services without an international air transport authority operating it, that authority merely licensing them, you have all the pressure of private ownership on rates to make all possible profit out of international air transport, and to that extent you have deprived the people of the world of some of the benefits of this modern means of travel which we feel should be secured to them.

I would point out also that under the terms of the draft convention we in this country would be putting public money into the providing of air fields and ground services of one kind or another for those international lines. I think it is of concern to us whether that is to result in increased private profit to privately owned companies in other countries, operating into Canada, or whether it is to result in increased benefit to the people of other countries and to the whole world. In other words, I want to urge upon the government that it should consider going a step further than it has in the agreement that has been tabled.
There are one or two points of detail in the draft convention that I should like to comment on briefly. For example, I feel that we should be given more detail as to the basis for determining the relative importance to each state of international air services and of each state to international air services. This matter is referred to in paragraph 4 of the summary, and also in article IV, section 1, of the convention, and article V, section 1 of the convention. On the basis of this relative importance will be determined the membership in the proposed assembly, the-membership of the board, and the membership of the regional council. It should be readily seen that this is a matter of great importance, and I feel that more detail should have been given. Obviously the basis cannot be determined solely with respect to population, solely with respect to geographical size or geographical location. A great many factors-enter into the picture. I repeat that some detail should have been given; that we should know just what the view of the Canadian government is on this matter.
Then with respect to trans-frontier services, or services between two contiguous countries, I feel that the convention leaves the matter not as clear as it might be. In some sections it says that services between two contiguous countries will be excepted from the provisions of this convention; in others it says that services between any two countries may be worked out by themselves subject to the provisions of this convention, including specifically the provisions with respect to licences.. I am making two points in that connection: first, that the matter should be made clearer-than it is; second, that two contiguous countries such as the United States and Canada should have a certain amount of latitude in making agreements for what are called trans-frontier services; at the same time they should be subject to review by regional councils such as are provided for in the convention. While it may seem logical for two-

War Appropriation-Transport
countries such as the United States and Canada not to be subject to such a review, if you allow these bilateral agreements all over the world you can very soon weaken the position of the regional councils and of the whole attempt to establish uniformity of service and standards throughout the world. If private firms in some countries are stumbling blocks in this matter and represent the reason why the government is a bit timid, I would urge that into a gathering of this kind governmental representatives should go, not with the compromise that they hope to come out with, but with the most desirable position, and if they have to compromise at least they will not have had to give away too much as a result of that situation.
I would therefore urge these points on the government with respect to the international aspect of this whole situation. Nevertheless I repeat what I said earlier, that as far as the draft convention goes-and I have not only digested it over the weekend but have enjoyed studying it-it seems to me it should have the support of this parliament.
May I now turn to the domestic side of the picture. I should like first of all to say that the pride which the minister expressed the *other day in Trans-Canada Air Lines, especially his pride in its splendid record of safety, is one that is shared by the people of Canada from coast to coast. We are all very proud of our own Trans-Canada Air Lines.
With respect to the announcement that the minister made the other day to the effect that railway companies must within a year after the conclusion of the European war divest themselves of their air lines, I want to say that although I am no defender of the present government, the Minister of Munitions and Supply is to be congratulated on at last having lost patience with the Canadian Pacific in this matter. He put on Hansard facts which are the basis of his having lost his patience, if I may put it that way. First of all, the position which Canadian Pacific Air Lines now holds in this country has been made possible, not by the Canadian Pacific Air Lines, but in the first instance by the pioneering which was done by bush pilots down through the years. The minister pointed out that the Canadian Pacific was not in the picture for a great many years. It came along with its huge financial resources and was able to buy up all but one of the private companies in the field. As a matter of fact, I believe, the one which they did not buy up was not organized at the time Canadian Pacific Air Lines came into the field, less than three years ago.

The minister also pointed out the other day, although in this instance I do not know whether he was condemning Canadian Pacific Air Lines or condemning himself, that whereas Trans-Canada Air Lines has been unable to get additional transport planes during the course of the war, somehow or other it has been possible for the Canadian Pacific Air Lines to get additional planes because of the work that it was doing on the northwest staging route. I am still puzzled about that. I feel that the minister not only should condemn Canadian Pacific Air Lines for what they have done in this connection, but should answer the question why it was possible for them to get extra planes and at the same time not possible for Trans-Canada Air Lines to do so. I understand they now have more planes than Trans-Canada Air Lines has, and this at a time when the United States commercial air lines are operating their present services with little more than half the number of planes they had at the outbreak of the war. This is an example of the special privilege which this company has enjoyed, and it is on the basis of this special privilege that they have been able to build up the huge monopoly they have at the present time. Not only have they exploited the war situation in this way, but Canadian Pacific Air Lines is playing on sectional interests in various parts of the country, getting municipalities and councils to send in resolutions of one kind and another, and doing everything it can be threaten the position of our own publicly owned Trans-Canada Air Lines.
The Minister of Munitions and Supply has had long experience of this kind of thing. He did not lose his patience overnight. I was interested in reading the other day some of the debate in 1937, to find this from the minister, as reported in Hansard of that year, pages 2216 and 2217. The Minister of Munitions and Supply is speaking:
The question now arises: Have we invited the private interests to participate? That question was asked. May I say we did not need to invite them. They came from every part of Canada and the United States, and put on the most persistent lobby in Ottawa that I have ever seen. The only way we could make progress was to absolutely refuse to talk to them. We said, "Go back home...."
I am glad, in view of the intervening experiences which the minister has had with private enterprise endeavouring to build up, on the basis of the efforts of little people, a huge monopoly, that the minister has taken the strong stand he has in this matter. Not only has Canadian Pacific Air Lines built up its strong position at the present time on the basis of the factors which I have laid down,

War Appropriation-Transport
but it has done so with considerable government assistance. The minister mentioned the other day the part which air mail contracts have played in the development of air service down through the years, and not many days ago he gave figures as to the amount of government money which is going into the building of routes such as that from Edmonton to Whitehorse. He gave the figure at that time as about S46,000,000. In addition to that $46,000,000 of capital cost, I have here information which was given in sessional paper No. 213 of this year when I asked for the annual operating cost of the Edmonton to Whitehorse route and also the annual revenues from companies flying over that route. In 1943 it cost the government, to maintain that route, $337,835.63. The total amount of revenue which the government received from the only private company flying over that route, which was the Yukon Southern Air Transport Limited, fully owned by the Canadian Pacific, was only $30,276.05. In other words, there simply is no such thing as private enterprise in the field of air transport; what you have is the government providing the air fields, the air routes, the meteorological services and the other things which are necessary to make possible the flying of these planes, at almost no cost to the private company; you have the bush pilots of the early days developing these routes; and then you have private finance in the hands of the Canadian Pacific coming along at the last minute and cashing in on the whole works.
It is quite interesting to note, in a Gallup poll which was published just a day or two ago, some figures with respect to this whole question. I know that if the hon. member for Broadview hears me mention "Gallup poll" he will put in his crack about it. Nevertheless the figures are interesting. A vote was taken by these people as to what the Canadian public wants in regard to the ownership of airlines, and these were'the figures: Government ownership, forty-four per cent; private ownership, eighteen per cent; a combination of both, twenty-eight per cent; undecided, ten per cent. If you take these figures, eliminating the ten per cent who do not know what they want and consider the rest, you find that only twenty per cent want unadulterated private ownership while the other eighty per cent want either government ownership or a combination of the two.
I suggest, therefore, to the Minister of Munitions and Supply and the government that they are moving in the direction of the thought of the Canadian people when they look away from private monopoly in air transport and toward the strengthening of the people's position as expressed in government ownership. But now, in spite of the fact that the minister has taken the stand he has, namely, that the principle of non-profit and non-competitive operation should rule in air transport, I am afraid that the proposal he made the other day, although we welcome it, does not go far enough. I refer to his statement that within a year after the war the Canadian Pacific Railway, for example, must divest itself of its ownership of airlines, and also his statement that from now on no licences to operate new routes will be given to any railway operating airlines.
That is good, but I cannot help reminding the committee of the fact that once upon a time the Aluminum Company of America found it necessary to divest itself of ownership of the Aluminum Company of Canada, and what did that mean? Simply, that it was transferred to Aluminium Limited, so that we still have the same people in the background operating what has become a world cartel and drawing to themselves the profits from that operation.
I suggest that this is the question to be looked at here. It is not good enough merely to tell the Canadian Pacific Railway that they must divest themselves of ownership of Canadian Pacific Air Lines. It will *still be possible, under a separate name, for a private monopoly to be built up comprising the tremendous hold that Canadian Pacific Air Lines now have, which not only will challenge the position of Trans-Canada Air Lines but will interfere with the principle which I have said is important, namely, that we should secure for the people of Canada the full benefit of this modern development of air transport.
I say, therefore, that on this domestic front the government should go considerably further, and I would suggest at least two or three steps which in my opinion should be taken. I believe, for example, that the northwest staging route from Edmonton to White Horse and on into Alaska should be taken over and made part of Trans-Canada Air Lines because of the importance of that route in flying to Asia. Similarly, I feel that the route down the Mackenzie, because of its importance in the development of Canada's northland, where so much mineral wealth is located, which by the way is largely under the control of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, with its Canadian Pacific Railway connection, should be nationalized and made part of Trans-Canada Air Lines. I would say the same about the route being developed to Labrador, which may become very important in the services to Europe.
War Appropriation-Transport

If I had time I would make further suggestions along this line, but certainly I suggest that the government should take further steps toward nationalizing these sections of the present Canadian Pacific Air Lines.
There are other matters I should like to discuss but my time will not permit. However, I would express concurrence in the idea of setting up an air transport board, and I am particularly pleased at the fact that it is to be not just a judicial body, but one that is to act as an instrument of government policy, and that its purpose will be to develop and foster the extension of air services, air fields, air routes, research into new kinds of planes, construction and so on. That should be the function of such a body. It should not be just a judicial or restrictive organization but a body which in the name of the people of Canada takes the initiative to develop these modern means of transportation to see to it that its full and richest benefits shall come to and be secured to the people of Canada as a whole.
My time is just about up and I shall draw to a close, but before I do so I should like to quote from a gentleman who was a member of this house some years ago and who had some views on this subject. I refer to the then Right Hon. R. B. Bennett. Speaking in 1937 in the debate on the Trans-Canada Air Lines bill, as reported at pages 2210, 2211 and 2212, of Hansard of that year, these are some of the things that Mr. Bennett said:
I submit that in the light of the experience we have had in this country, if we are going into this air line business, we should own it from the start and not later.
Mr. Woodsworth: Hear, hear.
Later on, Mr. Bennett had this to say:
But I do now implore the minister not to part with this property. To-night the field is clear. To-night no franchise encumbers the .ground. To-night we stand in a position to create by act of this parliament an enterprise that will have complete control of aerial navigation between the Atlantic and the Pacific. We have that right to-night. If we pass this measure-
That is, the bill in the form in which it stood at that time.
-and hand this right over, not to the crown, but to a body of shareholders and provide that the crown may buy it back sometime in the future if it so desires, we shall be going in the wrong direction. I plead with the minister to reverse the process, to own the enterprise nowr, and sell it later, if he so desires. That is the difference between the minister's view and mine of the principles that underlie this measure. 1 make this suggestion to the minister not because I can be said to be one of those who believe in public ownership and control, for I have not that reputation, but because I have found by grim experience that the condition
(Mr. Knowles.]
that now exists in Canada with respect to railroads has arisen in consequence of the blunder we made.
That was Mr. Bennett speaking.
We cannot make a blunder if we keep what we have got, and what we have got to-night is control of the whole matter. It seems to me, therefore, wise to take initial steps to ensure that that control shall be retained by the action of this parliament and if we desire later to terminate it or to part with it, we may do so through an act of this house and as a result of the intelligent expression of opinion by members of parliament.
I have no desire to go into the matter at greater length, nor do I wish at this moment to go into details, because that will have to be done in committee. But I do hope that the minister will not part with control as this bill provides-control which in my judgment is so essential to our success in view of all the difficulties that will confront us-and we shall then be in a position to cope with the situation in a manner that will be denied us if we adopt the principle of this measure.
As I understand it, Mr. Bennett was stating an obvious fact, that it is a great deal easier to hold on to what you have than it is to try to get it back afterwards, and I suggest to the minister and to the government that they have learned this from bitter experience even in the last year. It is less than a year since the Prime Minister made his very important statement of the government's policy with respect to civil aviation, at which time he made it clear that Trans-Canada Air Lines was to have the exclusive operation of Canada's main line services and also our international connections, but also at which time he said to private enterprise, "The whole north country is yours". In less than a year this private company has taken advantage of that position to build up this huge monopoly which challenges the position of the government to the point where, even against his will, the Minister of Munitions-I am assuming that it is against his will, although I cannot presume to know what goes on in his mind-has had to take this somewhat drastic action. I suggest that this shows what can happen in a very short time with these powerful monopolies. At the present time we have not lost it all. We own the route from Edmonton to Alaska and in certain other sections. There are areas where final franchises have not been given, where the whole question of what lines are to fly these international routes has not been, finally settled. We have not lost this as yet; but if we carry on the policy of saying to private enterprise, whatever monopoly it may be, Canadian Pacific Air Lines or under some other name, "That field is yours," the day will come when we shall regret not having held on to what we have at this time. Therefore I plead with the government, in the domestic field as

War Appropriation-Transport
on the international front, to look again at this whole programme as laid down in the statement made on Friday. It is good as far as it goes, and I hope we shall not hear from any part of this house any suggestion that the government should take any less of a step than, it proposes. But I would urge that it consider going further, both internationally and domestically, along the lines I have suggested.

speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I have seen the leader of the C.C.F. party play this old game of politics quite often, but I have never seen him in quite as good form as he is in to-day. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Like the leader of the opposition, I was not present when the statements were made on Friday evening. However, I do recall the statement on Thursday evening. As a result of that statement our party got together on Friday morning and discussed civil aviation, though we did not know what the minister was going to say that afternoon. The matter has been further discussed since that time, as should be quite evident from the comprehensive statement that has been made in behalf of this party, and before we came into the house this afternoon we discussed the matter further. I wish to say to the leader of the opposition that it seems to me unfortunate that we cannot proceed with this matter to-day as we had expected to be able to do. I must accept the word of the hon. gentleman that this is not because his party has been unable to arrive at a decision, but I think I have a right to draw my own conclusions as to what that reason may be, and I shall do so.
I just want to add that I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has placed our position before the committee clearly and ably. We do welcome this step. For a long time we have felt that future generations might regret it if we allowed the present situation in this country with regard to aviation to continue. This is a
War Appropriation-Transport

new mode of transportation. Many of us in this house have done a good deal of flying at one time or another, and we realize perhaps more fully than a great many of the general public that to-day the safety, rapidity and comfort of air transport are bound to have a tremendous effect on the future development of transportation generally.
Another consideration I have in mind is that in this country we have a railway system owned by the people and another owned by a great corporation, the shareholders of which are very largely beyond our borders and the shares and securities of which may come into our hands at the conclusion of the war, thus giving us control of that other great transportation system. I have believed for a long time that while perhaps two well-established organizations within the same transportation field might engage, not in competition in the usual sense but in friendly rivalry, so that one form or one organization may become a yardstick for another form or another organization, yet in a country like this, with its great distances, with the necessity of transportation to join one part of the country to the other, it is essential that we should have a closely integrated and well-knit transportation system. I am pleased to see that the government intends to retain control of this great new facility. I was present the night the former leader of the opposition in this house, the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, gave the warning which we can say to-day as we look back ought to have been heeded to a greater extent than has been the case. I am glad, therefore, to see that we have an opportunity now of controlling this great new form of transportation. Perchance, when the war is over, in the development of our country we shall have to consider ways and means of integrating all our transportation systems. I recall the years before the war when some hon. members talked about railway deficits, and when proposals were *made to tear up railway lines, mostly lines operating under the Canadian National Railways system. We were asked then to relieve ourselves of the financial burden those lines involved when, at the same time, we saw growing up in this country other and unregulated forms of public transportation.
These were, of course, the buses and trucks. We now have transportation by air. My view has always been that our transportation system, in a country like Canada, ought to be intelligently operated and intelligently integrated. For example, trucks and buses ought to be feeders to the railways upon which, to a great extent, because of the heavy freight we must carry long distances, the economic life

of this country must depend. That ought to be the situation, rather than have trucks and buses in disastrous competition with our railway systems. That means, of course, that if we are to have a desirable condition we must have the entire system under public rather than private control. The air arm, that great new field of transportation, most assuredly should be under national ownership and control now.
My colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has spoken of the international importance of air transportation. I believe we have to consider it not only from the point of view of domestic convenience but also from that of national security and world peace. In the last generation we have had an opportunity to see how civil air transportation has assisted great nations to lay the foundations of military air power. Particularly was that developed in Germany. So that when the war came we found that through her civil air transportation system and the civil training of her young men in the operation of aeroplanes and gliders, she had a potential air force ready and willing to destroy the rest of the world.
Accordingly in the field of international air transportation it becomes apparent and, I think, important, that only public control should function. International cooperation does not mean, in reality, a diminution of national sovereignty. What it really means is, sometimes, the transfer-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
-of national sovereignty between nations, and an expansion of it into a larger and wider field, so that a nation may have a voice in something greater and larger than its own narrow domestic affairs. I think in the field of civil aviation we must have international understanding, international operation and international control. I should like to see the world go beyond where I think it can go to-day. I should like to see an international system owned internationally; but I realize that under present world conditions not only is that improbable but it is quite out of the question. Hence I believe we must have an intergovernmental regulatory body, one which will license and regulate and enter into arrangements with the nations, so that we may achieve the results we desire, namely efficient transportation, rapid transportation, comfortable transportation, safe transportation-and peace at the end of it all.
I am glad, too. that the minister spoke as he did on Friday. I believe he made the position clear in that regards-because Canada is in a strategic position. The airways of the world cross our country-the airways to Europe,

War Appropriation-Transport
northeast and over the top of the world, or to the northwest, as we sometimes call it, again going near the cap of the world to Asia and into India. Those of us who have studied the new maps made in recent years showing the air routes of the world over the polar or arctic regions realize that instead of going in the direction in which we thought we should go, namely east or west, we went northwest, northeast, and sometimes even north to get to the places which seemed east or west of us.
As I say, Canada is in a strategic position. The airways to many parts of the world, from the great centres of population in North America to the continents of Europe and Asia, pass over this country. It is well, therefore, that an early start has been made by the government and by parliament in placing before other nations for their consideration the viewpoint-at least, I hope it is the viewpoint-of this entire country, regardless of our political affiliations. I should like to see our government extend air transportation as rapidly as possible into other parts of the world. As soon as we are able to do so, I should like to see Canada establish an air route to South America as well as to Europe and Asia. After all, we have much in common with the progressive peoples to be found in at least some of the South American countries, and there are advantageous trade relationships to be made between us. Therefore I welcome this step forward. I agree also with the criticisms which have already been made, but I think it is well that at this time we should face this great problem and let other nations of the world know where we stand.
In conclusion, may I say that Canada, as far as her population is concerned, is a small nation. But in the field of aviation she is a great nation-one of the three or four leading nations of the world. A great deal of pioneering has been done in Canada, and probably when the history of the war is written it will show that our greatest contribution will have been made in the air. Whether that be so or not, we have in Canada, I believe, a people who are air conscious to an extent greater than applies to people in most countries. We have tremendous opportunity in this field to wield an influence for good out of all proportion to our population or to our size. I hope we shall be able to make that position clear, and to maintain it when the time comes to negotiate agreements with other countries.

If we are to discuss
