maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: It is the place of the government to decide the order of business. At six o'clock we shall drop civil aviation and then go on with the discussion of munitions production. When we finish the munitions production discussion, we shall go back to civil aviation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Now we are getting back to what was my understanding on Friday evening. Perhaps I may be allowed to run over 
the facts as I see them. Last fall the minister returned from the United Kingdom after holding important conferences there. I remember distinctly reading in the press that he had not brought back a draft agreement on this matter but that he would make a statement in the house, obviously after the house opened. Eight weeks have passed and at last we have had the minister's statement. When that statement was delivered we understood clearly that the debate would not then ensue. On Friday night the minister who was speaking for the government explained what the business to-day would be in such a way that I, who had taken it up with him, understood that we were going into other portions of the statement of the Minister of Munitions and Supply. It was not until just before I came into the house this afternoon that I heard that the government had changed its decision and wanted to proceed with civil aviation and permit a debate on the minister's important statement to take place. That change was not entirely convenient to members of the opposition. The arrangement to which the minister is now ready to agree is entirely in accordance with our understanding Friday night and I think it satisfactorily solves the whole matter.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: If the proposal made a moment ago by the minister is carried out, docs it mean that at eight o'clock he will make a statement on other aspects of munitions and supply?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: No, to-morrow at three o'clock.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: What shall we do at eight o'clock tonight?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: I cannot say just what the exact programme will be.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Possibly item No. 5 on the order paper, which is a resolution standing in the name of the Minister of Finance to raise money by way of loan. Then we shall possibly take up the estimates of the Department of Public Works.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Civil supply.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: And then two items of supply, as announced on Friday night.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: I agree with the statement made by the Minister of Munitions and Supply that we should discuss items No. 1 and 2 and then leave item No. 3, which is civil aviation. Shall I call item No. 1 for discussion?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Just before you do that, I think someone should make it more clear what we are to take up at eight o'clock. I still do not understand the situation.

War Appropriation-Transport

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: I have stated that we shall take up item No. 5 on the order paper and then supply.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: What supply?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Public works and then two items in departments not called yet, Secretary of State and Munitions and Supply civil estimates. That was announced Friday evening.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Item No. 1:
1.	Radio services, $2,666,045.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Does this item cover services supplementary to the general radio services?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Yes, these estimates arise wholly out of the war. Many radio beams have been installed between military airports and to provide defence services on the coasts. These are operated by the Department of Transport for the military services. All the items under this heading will disappear when the war is over; they are for purely war services.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: There would be nothing under this item which would have to do with the short-wave system that is proposed?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: No; these are purely war estimates.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Under what item could I discuss the radio service between Winnipeg and Edmonton?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: That is a civil item which will be introduced later.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: The minister cannot say very much about these amounts, because they are secret?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Yes; they cannot be discussed in detail, I am afraid.

Item agreed to.
2.	Meteorological services, $1,670,480.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Is there any relationship between this and the meteorological service already carried on throughout Canada for purposes other than war?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: The situation is exactly the same. These are items that will disappear when the war ends. The services are installed wholly for war purposes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: They are not set up as separate stations from those in many instances already in existence and furnishing meteorological service, or are they entirely new stations set up for purposes of war?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
They are really expansions of that service for war purposes. WThen I said 100-105J
that all meteorological stations installed for war purposes would disappear as peace-time services, I should qualify that, because we have extended the range of activities in that field and we might wish to retain the extended range. For instance, we have stations along the arctic.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Would
some of those be taken over by the Trans-Canada service?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: I might read what it covers: Meteorological services for (a) Trans-Atlantic ferry service with Dorval as the main centre. There is no civilian Trans-Atlantic line. The . item includes teletype installed from Dorval to Newfoundland; (b) Eastern and western air commands and the fleet; (c) Northwest staging route from Edmonton or Vancouver through White Horse to the Alaskan boundary; (d) R.C.A.F. and R.A.F. transport command; (e) R.C.A.F. aeroplane ferry from Kapuskasing. These are services which may be replaced with sendees for other purposes, but at the moment they are part of the war service. For instance, the ferry command to the United Kingdom is a war service, and the meteorological service that accompanies it is-also a war service.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: These stations are built so that they can be taken over later on?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Yes. They are civilian stations,, operated by civilians. They are stations that would not be operated had the war not happened. As I say, we might operate them for another purpose after the war, such as the Atlantic ferry service. The only Atlantic ferry service Canada has to-day is a war service.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: The minister mentioned the Edmonton-Alaska staging route. If that sendee is to be taken over by civil aviation you would need the stations, would you not?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Yes. If there is a civilian plane service after the war, as I presume there will be, then this vote will be transferred to the civil vote and continued as civil aviation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Would not a service like that help your navy and navigation generally after the war, especially if a new route is opened up and you have planes not only inside the coast but on the coast?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
I presume there will be a civilian service after the war. The point I am making is that there are no civilian services there to-day and therefore this comes under the war vote and not a civil vote.
War Appropriation-Transport

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: The thought I had in mind was this: Have you in mind all the time that some of these stations will be taken over on a permanent basis?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Yes. We are working with a single purpose in mind at the moment; we are working for war.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: I know that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: We are mindful of the fact that facilities installed for war will undoubtedly be required for peace.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Has the minister a break-down showing the cost of the service in the northwest staging route, and how much the Canadian Pacific Air Lines pay for the meteorological services supplied by the Department of Transport?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: The estimate for the meteorological work included in this item on the northwest staging route is $317,000. I may say that no one pays for weather service. Weather service is paid for by the government as a service to all aviation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: With respect to the minister's statement that the meteorological services would disappear after the war, may I say that I cannot see it in that way. I am interested in the Trans-Canada Air Lines plane service made available to Sydney since the war. That service serves the whole area around that section of the country. They land on a R.C.A.F. field which is a large well-developed field for war purposes. In effect the minister's statement is. that that service would disappear when the war is over. That, would mean a discontinuation of the Trans-Canada Air Lines plane service now available in that area because of the war.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: May I clarify that? My hon. friend is speaking of a service that is not included in this vote. That is a civil aviation service and it is paid for out of the civil vote. This is a war vote.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Does the item of $1,670,480 cover the purchase of a considerable number of instruments for this purpose?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: This is primarily the cost of operating.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Where would the instruments come in?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Material, supplies and equipment, $157,000, are included in this item.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Is there a vote elsewhere for more instruments than the minister has just mentioned?
(Mr. Howe.]

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: That is all. I can read the break-down of the item: salaries, $784,723; war duty supplements-I may say that applies to the war vote-$244;860; cost of living bonuses, $64,000; living allowances, $55,360; contributions to unemployment insurance fund, $5,000; weather observer contracts, $21,490; telephone and telegrams, $31,000; teletype, $110,000; travelling expenses, $32,000; printing and stationery, $28,000; materials, supplies and equipment, $157,000; construction, $59,000; freight, express and cartage, $62,000; sundries, $16,047. That makes a total of $1,670,480.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: In reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Mackenzie a little while ago the minister said that private air lines did not pay for meteorological services. May I ask on what basis payment is made to the government by private air lines over such a route as the northwest staging route? What services do they pay for in the figure that I gave earlier this afternoon? The figure I referred to for 1943 was roughly $30,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Payment is made on the basis of a fee for each landing. Each time a plane lands at an airport it pays a fee for doing so. It also pays for the communication sendees from the plane to the ground; that is the telephone and telegraph services from the plane to the ground. Where the government owns the ground station, each message which it receives from a plane carries with it a fee. These are a means of obtaining revenue from privately-owned planes or Trans-Canada planes. All planes flying pay the same scale of fees.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: I suppose one can say that the whole of the meteorological services in connection with such fields as Gander and Goose come under this vote?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: What about those which were carried on for Hudson bay and Hudson bay strait and localities up there? Are they still carried on, and come under this?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
No; they come under a civil vote. If they were established before the early days of the war they come under a civil vote. It has been thought wise not to increase the civil vote by purely war expenditures. The purpose is, after the war is over, to consider what is then required as a permanent service and then to establish the civil vote. But the services which were in operation prior to the war are all charged to the civil vote.

War Appropriation-Transport

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Is all the information collected by the meteorological service- I mean from all over the place, civil facilities, the army, and the air force-gathered together and the results tabulated?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Yes; all the meteorological data is gathered and supplied to one source and distributed from the one source. There is no division of the meteorological service.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Perhaps under this item the question might be discussed as to the publication of weather forecasts across Canada. If my memory serves me correctly, at the beginning of the war weather forecasts were not made. Then some change was instituted which permitted certain localities to provide forecasts. I notice weather forecasts appear as a matter of course in practically every newspaper, at least newspapers which I happen to get in this district. Are weather forecasts made public generally throughout the country?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Whether the weather forecasts can be made public is a security matter which is determined by the chiefs of staff of the armed forces. Weather forecasts in certain areas, particularly in the Atlantic, are of importance to the enemy.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: I understand that some of the services included in this item are available to Trans-Canada Air Lines and to the Canadian Pacific as well as to the armed forces.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Yes; they are available to anyone. All the information collected on weather is available not only to Canadians but to everyone in the United States. Similarly all the weather information which is gathered in the United States is made available to Canada. There is a constant stream of weather information going out to every air field in the country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: This is treated exactly the same as in the case of water navigation?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
What percentage of the
operating personnel included in this vote is civilian and what is in the services?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: All those under this vote are civilians.

Item agreed to.
S. Civil aviation:
Extra airport traffic control systems, $736,450; operation and maintenance of municipal (terminal) airports, $398,260; additional facilities, Moncton to Newfoundland airline, $130,500 (revote $78,500); improvements to airports,
$500,000; Canadian government transatlantic air service, $400,000; total, $2,243,710.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Docs the first of these items cover certain airports, traffic in certain airports, remembering always that it is the war expenditure portion of traffic control?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
The following is the estimate of the funds required for the operation of three airway traffic control centres and fourteen airport control towers and an interphone and teletype service to control and direct the movement of aircraft on the airways and on approaches to landing of the various terminal airports in Canada.
This service was inaugurated in 1939 as a protective measure for airline and Royal Canadian Air Force aircraft, but during the past years has been greatly extended to meet the increased requirements made necessary by: the enlarged training programme of the R.C.A.F.; the expansion of the ferry command services of the Royal Air Force, the Royal Canadian Air Force, and the United States Army Air Force; the increased activity of the air transport command of the United States Army Air Force; the operation of traffic control centres and airport control towers on a twenty-four hour basis; the extension of interphone and teletype installations to provide a continuous service covering approximately 5,500 miles of airways from Vancouver, British Columbia to Torbay, Newfoundland; from Edmonton to Lethbridge, Alberta; from Montreal to Quebec; from North Bay, Ontario to Winnipeg, Manitoba; from Winnipeg, Manitoba, via Saskatoon to Edmonton; from Toronto via Sault Ste. Marie to Winnipeg; also to points in the United States, to connect with circuits provided by the civil aeronautics division of the United States. Such teletype facilities to include service between Winnipeg, Manitoba, and Pembina, Minnesota; Edmonton, Alberta, and Coutts, Alberta; Vancouver, B.C. and Blaine, Washington. Airway and airport traffic control stations are located as follows: airway traffic control centres, Winnipeg, Toronto and Montreal; air traffic control towers, Vancouver, Lethbridge, Edmonton, Calgary, Regina, Saskatoon, Winnipeg, Windsor, North Bay, Toronto, London, Ottawa, Montreal and Moncton.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Are you dealing with
these subclause by subclause?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: I am waiting for No. 4.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: I called the whole item, thinking the discussion would be general.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Subclause 1 is carried, Mr.. Chairman?

War Appropriation-Transport

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Subclause 1 is carried. We shall now deal with subclause 2, operation and maintenance of municipal airports, $398,260.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Would the minister explain this one?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Yes. This item is for the operation and maintenance of fourteen municipal and other airports owned or leased by the Department of Transport for the duration of the w'ar, all of which are being utilized by the air forces of Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States for training operations, namely, Vancouver, Lethbridge, Winnipeg, London, Charlottetown, Edmonton, Medicine Hat, Fort William, Malton, Buchan, Calgary, Regina, Windsor, New Glasgow. This service was taken over by the Department of Transport from the Department of National Defence air services on April 1, 1912, and has since been maintained with funds provided by allotment from war appropriation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
In view of the fact that
a great many districts are planning now for after the war business, in the way of developing district airports-I have in mind now the counties of Waterloo, Perth, Wellington and, I think, Huron, with some of the surrounding counties, the idea being to develop an airport which will take in the towns within a radius of thirty-five or forty miles, andi will prove important in the development of these districts- is the department now making any plans? I realize that some will come under reconstruction and* the repatriation of our men coming back, giving them work and so on; 'but is the department making plans whereby these developments, with government assistance, can be coordinated into the general scheme which undoubtedly we shall have when the war is over.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: The government is not encouraging new development of airports at this time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: I do not mean now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: We are willing, at the request of a municipality, to survey a site and report on it to the municipality, and then advise the municipality whether or not it is wise to purchase the land. But we are not prepared to make a commitment to any municipality about the nature of government assistance that will follow.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
The department has been of great assistance to us in our district. It has sent a man there who has made surveys and helped us in every possible way; he is a

very able fellow. We do think, however, that perhaps it is not too early to start on a plan for that work, because the big industrial centres such as we have in Waterloo, Perth, Welling' ton and that district dare not be off the air line. When the war is over we must be on the air line if we are to continue the development that has been built up over the last fifty or sixty years. Possibly it might be a good idea to have this whole picture coordinated with the efforts of the Department of Labour and other departments of government so that they may look after the post-war development of the country. I do not think it is too early to start and make some of these plans and have a general survey by the department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: The department is studying the situation, but municipal airports are usually started by the efforts of the municipality, and usually it is the municipality that puts the steam in the particular problems. The department either helps or vetoes as arrangements work into the general plan. I must say that until the war is further advanced we shall have to ask the municipality to do the pushing, requesting the government for such help as it requires from time to time which does not involve help in the actual construction of the airport.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Can the minister interpret the term "municipal"? He mentioned Regina. Does the city of Regina own that airport?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
On what terms does the
government take over an airport and operate it?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: At the beginning of the war we made an arrangement that all municipal airports required by the government for war purposes would be rented from the municipality at one dollar a year, the government undertaking to pay all operating expenses and make such improvements in the airports as might be required for war purposes. The municipalities that .entered into that arrangement have profited by it considerably, because all airports have been materially extended to meet the requirements of the air training plan.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Will these improvements be turned back to the municipality?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: The question is being considered. I may say that the land belongs to the municipality.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
But the improvements belong to the dominion government?

War Appropriation-Transport

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: The improvements usually go with the land.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
If I may say a word touching the point raised by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth), I appreciate the minister's position with regard to the war coming first, and I think we all agree with that. But he also qualified that in one of his remarks, when he said that he is not unmindful of what comes afterwards. That is the proper attitude to take. The whole problem of transportation by air will be a very serious matter for many of the centres throughout Canada, because what happened when the railways went through the country may very well happen in connection with air lines. Those places which were on the railway lines were the ones that afterwards became great cities or impcrtant centres in Canada. The same situation m^y develop in connection with air lines; we may have a parallel here. In those days when the railways were pioneering their way through the dortlinion, the places which the roads did not go through gradually subsided in influence, in population and in business, and other centres which were on the main line of transportation took their place. Most of us envisage in the years that lie ahead the magnificent development that will take place in connection with air lines, and, I think the minister might give further consideration to the whole question of integrating, by way of survey and plan across Canada, the efforts of the government with respect to air lines in the days after the war.
I have been greatly impressed by the suggestion of the hon. member for Waterloo South in that particular respect. It is important that the minister give special consideration to it, because some of these towns and other places which to-day are thriving business sections may perhaps, if they are not properly integrated into an air line system, find that the present system of transportation may not meet the requirements of business which will come in another decade. They may find the whole situation changed. I add my word to what the hon. member has said.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: I covered that phase of the matter fully in my statement on Friday. When my hon. friend recovers from his long weekend he will read the statement and find that the point is covered.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: A number of air force stations are being closed at the present time. This year, I believe, the plans are that some twenty-eight are to be closed. The people are concerned about the use that is to be made of these airports, the buildings and other facilities.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: I wish to apologize to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon). I have some information and I realize that my remark was very much out of place and very rude. I apologize to him. I was trying to be amusing without any knowledge of the facts, and I hope he will forgive me.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: I did not think twice of that because I know my hon. friend would not have been rude intentionally.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: There are about twenty-eight airports that are being closed out by the Royal Canadian Air Force this year across Canada. People are somewhat concerned as to the best use that can be made of equipment and so on and would like to see those places continued as airports in peace time if possible. They have not the full knowledge of the facts, and I would urge on the minister and the government the importance of letting them know at the earliest moment whether or not there is any possibility of the present facilities and equipment being put to civilian use in aviation. It would be a tragedy if they were informed that it was not likely that a port could be used and then later on found that it would have been very valuable. I should like to see the government come forward with a long range plan to help these communities in the great job of reconstruction.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
I assure my hon. friend that airports that are being declared surplus to the air training plan will be maintained until the end of the war, and then as many of them as can be will be incorporated into the civil air services. As I stated on Friday, it is quite impossible to undertake new air services at this time. In the first place we have not the equipment, and in the second place we wish to wait and make the expansion of civil aviation part of the demobilization plans. I can assure my hon. friend, however, that the airports will not be allowed to deteriorate.
Progress reported.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: LOAN OF SI ,000,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES

speechtext:
Mr. D. C. ABBOTT (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
Government Loan

Resolved, tliat the governor in council be authorized to raise by way of loan under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, an amount not to exceed in the whole the sum of one thousand million dollars for paying or redeeming the whole or any portion of loans or obligations of Canada and also for purchasing unmatured securities of Canada and- for public works and general purposes.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: LOAN OF SI ,000,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether the parliamentary assistant desires to make a statement explaining this resolution now, or when we go into committee. I think, however, it might more properly be done now.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: LOAN OF SI ,000,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I am prepared to do that. This resolution is to renew the general borrowing authority of the government. The last loan act was passed in the 1942 session of parliament, and of the amount so authorized there remains unborrowed and negotiable $92,413,058. To December 31, 1944, there matures or is callable a total of $1,032,240,470.85, which is exclusive of the deposit certificate and treasury bills. Therefore, as the house appreciates, the bill following this resolution is to authorize borrowing power to enable the government, if necessary, to renew the various loans to which I have referred, totalling something in excess of a billion dollars.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Bradette in the chair.

maintopic: LOAN OF SI ,000,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I did not catch any reference by the parliamentary assistant to the last words of the resolution, namely "for public works and general purposes". What does the government propose to do with regard to that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: LOAN OF SI ,000,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: No, I did not refer to that. This resolution is in the same form as the resolution introducing a similiar bill in 1942. The money is borrowed under authority to be given under this measure, and can also be used for public works and general purposes of the government of Canada. It is to be noted, however, that the proceeds from sale of securities issued under this authority have to be paid into the consolidated revenue fund, and they can be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund only under some parliamentary authority. This means that the money borrowed under this measure can be used only for public works and general purposes if the moneys for those purposes have been voted or authorized by parliament. In previous loan acts, those of 1942, 1940, 1939, 1936, 1935, 1933 and 1931 there was provision that money borrowed could be used for public works and general purposes. There is no change in principle in this measure with regard to that matter.

maintopic: LOAN OF SI ,000,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Would the hon. member for St Antoine-Westmount be kind enough to tell me if the Bank of Canada will have anything to do with it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: LOAN OF SI ,000,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Well, the Bank of Canada acts as fiscal agent for the government. With that exception, however, I must say I do not quite understand what my hon. friend's question means. But except to the extent that the Bank of Canada acts as fiscal agent for the government in connection with the issue, registration and so on of government loans, I would say no.

I should like to put a question to the parliamentary assistant to the minister. Just exactly where is it proposed to obtain this money? Is it intended to obtain the money by floating bonds, or is it to be obtained from the chartered banks or from the Bank of Canada? I ask that question for this reason. We in this group have always advocated that to the extent that money obtained by taxation and by borrowing the legitimate savings of the people fails to meet government expenditures, the government should obtain funds from the Bank of Canada instead of borrowing from the chartered banks. Whether you obtain money from the Bank of Canada or from the chartered banks, in either ease it means expansion of money and to that extent it may be inflationary.
The argument of the Minister of Finance in the past has been that while you can
Government Loan

obtain money from the chartered banks without causing inflation, the obtaining of money from the Bank of Canada would be more inflationary. When money is borrowed from the Bank of Canada and paid out into circulation, eventually it finds its way to the chartered banks and thereby increases the cash reserves of the banks, making it possible for them to expand their loans by ten times the amount. When the parliamentary assistant spoke on the Industrial Development bank bill the other day he contradicted that statement. He said that there was no danger of inflation because the Bank of Canada would be able to control that situation. He referred to the statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard who had referred to the fact that if a certain amount of money was obtained from the Bank of Canada and paid out in circulation, apparently that would be increasing the cash reserves of the banks and thereby make it possible for them to expand their loans; The parliamentary assistant took the stand that that was not necessarily so because the Bank of Canada could take the necessaiy action to control the chartered banks in expanding their loans.
Mr. ABBOTT; I said that the amount of loanable funds involved in the proposed Industrial Development bank was not of such a magnitude that the central bank could not control the reserves of the chartered banks, even if the full amount went out into the commercial banking system. I think the statement made by the former chairman of the advisory committee on post-war reconstruction was far more practical in this regard. I should like to quote from the report of the special committee of the Senate in the session of 1943. The quotation will be found at page 29 of proceedings of the special committee, No. 1. This is what Doctor James had to say:
I wanted to add one further point there, namely, that the recognition of that policy of public investment as a marginal factor to take up the slack of private investment at any period implies the necessity of a complete change in our budget philosophy. We should still have an annual budget for probable revenues and expenditures; but so far as public investment expenditures are concerned for the construction Of all kinds of projects, it would obviously be necessary to have a budget which extends over a period of years. Mr. Churchill two Sundays ago suggested four years as a period for a plan. That may be perfectly right, politically thinking, but economically 1 prefer a period of seven or ten years. It may also be true-I mention this because somebody may think of it-that the adoption of that policy will mean a slight but continuous increase in the total public debt of Canada over the next hundred years.
The only exception I take to that statement is this: Why say one hundred years? Why not say "forever as long as we continue on the present system"? If under a policy of that kind whereby you can maintain the full development of the resources of the nation you will have a continued debt for the next one hundred years, I should like to know how you are going to pay off the national debt in the manner suggested in the quotation from the predecessor of the present Minister of Finance? I think we should adopt a practical attitude toward this whole thing. Come out frankly and say that we are going to continue under the present system, which means a continuous increase in debt forever and when the debt gets so large we can no longer service it we will borrow money and pay interest on it. Let us be frank about it. If we are to carry on under such a system it will mean a continued increase in the borrowing until the system will become so absurd that the people will realize there must be a change. On the other hand, if we are really sincere in wanting to bring about a reduction in the national debt, let us recognize that the only possible way by which we can ever bring it about is by the issue of debt-free money, because you cannot pay debt with debt.

speechtext: We have been talking a good deal about the details of facts and figures, but one big question remains when this is all boiled down. How much are the people of Canada in debt? After all, that is the great question that has to be answered. What is the per capita debt of the people of Canada, and how is that debt to be retired? It seems to me that sums up the whole thing. I am not so much concerned about where the Canadian National Railways debt is placed, or how many bond issues there have been in past years. As the representatives of the people we want to know how far our people are in debt; we want to know when the debt is to be paid off, and how. The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance is standing up to it well to-night; perhaps he will be Minister of Finance one of these days if he keeps going, and I hope this question does not embarrass him; but we should like to know how the government, if it remains in power, is to retire the debt. If the government cannot answer that question, let them tell the country so; let them get out of the saddle, and let somebody get in who knows how. That is the position. Perhaps we shall have an opportunity to challenge the Progressive Conservative party with the same question. If the parliamentary assistant, will answer that he is going to settle everything.

This is found at page 80 of report No. 1 of the banking and commerce committee. The question was asked:
Is it possible for you to imagine any way by which we are ever going to pay the debt we have got?
The debt at that time was only about three and a half billion dollars. This is what I find in the report:
Mr. Towers: As the debts of the government are an asset of the Canadian people, I do not see much point in, the thing; except that, to the extent that the government thinks that the distribution of those assets of the Canadian people-which are its debt-is unsatisfactory, it may take steps to remedy that distribution in any way that lies within the legislative power; in fact, in any way, I suppose-by income tax or succession duties or any other action it cares to take.
Then, further on in the report he said that the national debt, to a large extent, is a sign of a nation's prosperity. Take central Africa,

Government Loan
with no debt, and no prosperity. We should, therefore, be getting very prosperous in the future, because now our national debt has gone up to around eleven billions. It is increasing by about two and a half billions this year. If the war goes on for another two years our national debt will be around fourteen or sixteen billions.
The governor of the Bank of Canada could not tell us how we were to pay off the national debt of three and a half billions of dollars, so that I do not think he will know how we shall pay off a national debt of fourteen or sixteen billions. Yet, according to the sessional paper tabled in the house and referred to by me a few minutes ago, a scientific scheme is to be brought down by which this debt can be paid.
The .point I wish to raise is this:	I notice
that the national resources planning board of the United States, quoted by Stuart Chase in his book "Where Will the Money Come From," stresses the fact that there is no immediate danger until the national debt is equal to double the national income. Well, we shall be pretty near that in another two years, if our national debt gets up around fourteen or fifteen billions of dollars, and the national income falls to about seven billions.
Then they go on to say, and this is an. interesting point, that when the national debt rises to double the national income we shall probably have to use interest-free money in the future. Why wait until we reach, a crisis to use interest-free money? Why not use it before that? If it is possible to use interest-free money when we reach a crisis, in which the national debt is double the national income, then surely we can start to do so now and avoid this great interest-bearing debt.
Mr. Towers poinst out that the dangerous feature is not so much the size of the debt as the distribution of it. Are we bringing about a better distribution? The parliamentary assistant will probably say that to-day we are having a very wide distribution of bonds. But are we bringing about an equitable distribution of bonds? In respect of the third, fourth and fifth victory loans one-third of one per cent of the subscribers purchased sixty per cent of the total loan. This shows what a very inequitable distribution of debt we have to-day. So that in the future you will have to tax the whole population in order to pay tribute to a comparatively small number of people. Since the war we have greatly aggravated the problem to which the governor of the Bank of Canada referred. I am not referring to the size of the debt, but to the distribution of it, in which there is a more inequitable distribution of debt from day to day, as the war goes on. It is high time some action was taken.

maintopic: LOAN OF SI ,000,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES

The parliamentary assistant blames the war for the rise in. debt. May I point o.ut .that in 1934, for instance, the national debt of Canada was $3,141,042,097. At that time 44-11 per cent of our total revenue was used to pay interest on our national debt. That was in 1934. There was no war at that time, and I say that the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance is on the spot when he is asked to tell us how this debt is to be paid off.
If governments in the past were unable to meet their debt obligations, except by piling up more debt, then we doubt that this government, following the policy it has followed, will be able to pay off the debt, when it has already reached over ten billions of dollars. The people of Canada, and hon. members are entitled to a definite answer. The people want to know how the government is to retire this debt, because our children will have to bear the burden. If after the war the people have to spend seventy-five cents out of every dollar collected in taxes to pay the interest on our national debt, how in the world is the government to pay for all the social services, and all the promises which are being made during this session? Although it may be quite a job for the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance to answer this question he should, however, tell this committee and the people how the government intends to pay off the debt which the people will have to meet.

I rise to my feet at this time largely because of a remark made by the hon. member for York South who referred to 
the possibility of victory bonds being worth less than par at some time in the future. This matter was discussed during a previous debate, and I thought it was made fairly clear that the only real danger so far as these bonds were concerned was the possibility, remote though it may be, that the party of which the hon. member was a member would at some time get into power.
