maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE

speechtext: Mr. D. C. ABBOTT (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
On Friday, March 18, I promised that at the earliest opportunity I would reply to the Prime Minister's attack of March 10 upon certain remarks of mine of March 7, in which I said I believed that the quality and price of sugar in Canada had been manipulated by a trust or combine. I have no doubt the vested interests of Canada are highly gratified with the Prime Minister's vigorous defence of their prerogatives, and the reputedly richest man in Canada, J. W. McConnell, of Montreal, must be indebted to the Prime Minister for his eloquent testimonial of that gentleman's patriotism. I raised no question as to Mr. McConnell's patriotism. I raised, a question
Beet Sugar Industry

which the Prime Minister could have answered "yes" or "no"; but he did not answer that question. I did ask several other questions. The question which the people of Canada have a right to have answered is the one which I did submit to the Prime Minister. May I repeat the questions which I asked? I turn to page 1278 of Hansard and I find this is the question I asked:
What is the relationship existing between the government and this great sugar combine, and between the government and the head of this corporation, one John W. McConnell?
That is the first question. The second question is:
Why has the government condoned this manipulation in the sugar industry? It would allay considerable suspicion in this house and throughout the country if the Prime Minister would rise and categorically state that the Liberal party has never received, directly or indirectly, from the St. Lawrence Sugar Refining Company, from J. W. McConnell, or from anyone representing either or both of these, or any other Canadian sugar interest any contribution of money for the campaign funds of the Liberal party.
The answer to that question could have been given as either "yes" or "no". The Prime Minister must have known the answer. He did not choose to give the answer. I am sorry he is not in his seat at the present time.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions [DOT]rnd Supply):
maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can assure my hon. friend that the Prime Minister did not know and I do not know. The members of the government do not handle campaign funds.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: They know where they come from.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: Who does?

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: They ought to know.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
We have that much at least, whatever it means. The question arose out of my expression of belief that efforts were successfully -made before and during the present war to restrict artificially the production of beet sugar in Canada so that the cane sugar interests might prosper at the expense of the people, prosper not only through prices but through having the Canadian market reserved for their cane sugar. It is a fact which is perhaps not as well known throughout Canada as it might be that the cane sugar interests are desperately anxious to reserve the Canadian market for their own product; and consequently they will go to almost any limit in order to avoid having beet sugar production increased in the Dominion of Canada, and from that very fact we are suffering to-day.

May I give some evidence upon which I base my suspicion that the production of beet sugar in Canada has been deliberately restricted by the Liberal government ever since that government came into power. First of all I wish to read into the record a statement which perhaps is almost forgotten by a good many, showing that the Liberals had no excuse for neglecting the beet sugar industry in Canada. In 1932, in this house, under the administration of the Right Plon. R. B. Bennett, there was appointed a select standing committee on agriculture to conduct an investigation into the beet sugar industry. These men, among whom were a good many Liberals, did a thorough job. They called many reputable witnesses. After having conducted what they considered to be a thorough probe, they submitted a report in which the following words appear: I quote from Hansard, 1932, pages 1606 and 1607:
Your committee therefore recommend that in view of the existing tariff on sugar and in consideration of the substantial payments being made to agriculture and labour by the beet sugar factories at present in operation, 111'-cane sugar refineries should undertake to provide for a gradual increase in factory facilities for the refining of beet sugar in Canada, ami that, with the additional advantages in freight rates to points in the middle west, heretofore described, factory facilities should now be steadily increased in western areas where beets are grown, and thereby make it possible to produce from beets a more substantial percentage of the sugar consumption of Canada.
Your committee further recommends that if no successful attempt be made in the immediate future by the refineries to increase the facilities for the manufacture of beet sugar, the government should take into consideration steps to accomplish that end.
I had thought that it should be worth while to bring in the names of the Liberals who were on that committee. However, I will omit to mention them to-night. But there were a number of hon. members in this house in 1932. before the many labour-saving devices which have been brought into the beet sugar industry had been introduced, and therefore before beet sugar could be manufactured nearly as cheaply as can be done nowadays, who were advocating an increase in the production of beet sugar.
I have in my hand a brief which was prepared by the present parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Martin). That parliamentary assistant prepared a very fine brief; it did him credit. He was in favour of increasing the beet sugar production in Canada. ' Unfortunately his labours, since I have been here, have been so arduous that they have prevented him from getting round to the point of making a speech in support of beet sugar, although several times, while I have been speaking, he has kindly interjected remarks

Beet Sugar Industry
which indicated that he was sympathetic with my point of view, and I am sure he continues to be sympathetic.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: Undoubtedly most of the information in the hon. gentleman's speech comes from my brief.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
Undoubtedly; I seek knowledge wherever I can find it. I wish the Liberals would do the same. The trouble with the Liberals is tiiat they think that anything which does not come from Liberals is not , worth listening to.
I find on page 41 of that brief the following words:
It is not too much to ask of the federal government a definite consideration of the problem that will bring about a heavier consumption of beet sugar in Canada, thereby providing Canadian farmers with a greater income resulting from readier cash crops...
Furthermore, the government might well consider an advertising campaign to stimulate the use of ibeet sugar. In this way the unfair prejudice against beet sugar would gradually, but effectively, be eliminated.
These words do the hon. member great honour. This brief was submitted to the Hon. C. A. Dunning, then Minister of Finance, and to the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), at a conference held in the office of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) on Thursday, March 5, 1936, at eleven o'clock. I was present at that time. I think the Liberals cannot beg that they just did not know how important the beet sugar industry was in Canada: they cannot offer that plea in excuse. The Minister of Agriculture in the spring of 1937 sent Doctor E. S. Archibald out west to examine the beet sugar industry in Alberta. Whether the minister did that merely in order to make a fine gesture or whether he really wanted to find out what were the conditions in the industry, no one is able to say. But . Doctor Archibald went out, conducted an examination and came back and submitted, on October 28, 1937, a thorough and comprehensive report, in which he showed the great value of the beet sugar industry to Canada. He did not make any definite recommendation.
I have often wondered why. I have often wondered whether the reason he made no recommendation was that a certain thing had occurred in the spring of 1937, to which I shall refer by and by.
The Alberta Cooperative Sugar Beet Growers' Association made a submission to the Row^ell-Sirois commission, exhaustive and unanswerable in its arguments. Anyone who read that brief would realize that the beet sugar industry, at least in the west, was one which could not possibly be with impunity disregarded. It proves that the industry is economic and a success in every way. From page two of the report I read the following quotation:
To indicate the value of this industry to the agriculture of our district, the community in general and the Dominion of Canada, we submit the*following figures relating to the 1937 beet crop:
235,481 tons of .beets were produced from 19,829 acres of irrigated land-dn average of 11-88 tons per acre.
75,603,700 pounds of sugar were manufactured.
3,813 pounds was the per acre yield of refined sugar.
$3,040,000 worth of sugar was manufactured.
$155 was the total gross return per acre.
$77.50 was the gross return to the manufacturer.
$77.50 was the gross return per acre to the farmer.
The farmers' costs approximated $60 per acre which includes $25 per acre for hand labour 'by the farmer. These figures were given in a speech made by T. George Wood, Manager, Canadian Sugar Factories Limited, at Lethbridge, Wednesday, March 23,	1938. We
believe that this land is producing more food value per acre than any other land in the dominion.
Sugar beets of the highest quality can be grown, harvested and manufactured into refined sugar on all of our irrigated lands in Alberta. This industry has, in the districts where it is established, made a tremendous contribution toward the prosperity of both the urban and rural sections and to our national economy.
The annual returns .from the Lethbridge northern irrigation district rose from $761,000 m 1935 to $1,057,000 in 1936, the first year the new sugar factory operated in that territory.
If that year is in any way an indication of the ordinary performance of the beet sugar industry in Alberta, it is to be seen that the statement that the beet sugar industry is an economic success cannot possibly be refuted.
Something comes into the picture which is astonishing and which, I think, reflects great discredit upon the Liberal government and opens the way for the suggestion which I made the other day. In London, between April 5 and May 6, 1937, was held an international sugar conference. In that conference someone-and I have never been able to find out -who it was-is quoted as having said the following:
At the same time the government of Canada reiterates the assurance already given, that they do not propose to stimulate the production of sugar in Canada during the term of this agreement-
I interpolate here the remark that five years was the length of the agreement.
-by subsidy, increased protection, special remission of taxes, or by any other similar measure.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
Whom is the agreement between?
Beet Sugar Industry

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: Apparently it was a world agreement for the restriction of the production of sugar.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: Who was the author of that statement?

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: That is what we all w'ant to know. We have been trying to find that out since the statement was made and we cannot find out. Canada, astonishing as it may seem, the government of Canada, has held itself bound by that statement, as though the statement w'ere its bond. Who made that statement for Canada? That is an important question.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: Who represented Canada at the meeting?

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: We cannot find that out. I have tried to find out and I have put a question on the order paper. Who gave him the authority? We want to know that. Was the consent of the cabinet given in any resolution? Was any province consulted? Was this statement submitted to the cabinet after it was made? Was it passed? Was it submitted to any province? Was it submitted to parliament? As far as I can judge, the answer to every one of these questions would be no. Now, who is this individual, who sent him there, and under whose influence did he agree to that convention? That is the question that has to be answered.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: He is the little man who wasn't there.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
Well, his works remain; his tracks are there. If the answers to each of those questions must be no, then what? I think when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount (Mr. Abbott) finish explaining that matter they will remove a lot of suspicion in this country, and I think the Prime Minister will not be so eager to rush into parliament and accuse me of irresponsible utterances.
What did the United States do with respect to that agreement? The representative of the United States signed the agreement, and then the house of representatives and the senate of the United States repudiated it, refused to ratify it. Can anyone give me any reason why the United States, after signing the agreement, should refuse to ratify it, while Canada, without having signed it, would hold herself bound by the thing? If there was not some secret influence at work it is going to be pretty hard to make any hard-headed man believe it. It is astonishing.
Let it be borne in mind that in that year the war clouds were already threatening. Any
fMr. MacNicol.]
man of vision could see that war was coming; any man with judgment could see it. Furthermore, any man of vision, with any kind of information, would know that the war which was coming would be a war of bombs, of surface raiders, a war of submarines, and that consequently the sugar supply of Canada would be seriously threatened and that the sugar supply of the world would be destroyed. And anyone who reflected on Canada's happy position would realize that this country was in an admirable position to become the sugar-bowl for the needy world. Yet what was done?
The question springs into my mind:	Was
the government in its sugar policy, with respect to beet sugar, accommodating friends, or was it placating potential enemies? When I asked whether or not the Liberal party had received campaign funds from these gentlemen I was not insinuating that the Liberal party would necessarily be doing a reprehensible thing if it had received campaign funds.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: Oh, they would never do that.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
I was not implying
that. What I was indicating was simply this- what the Prime Minister apparently failed to get. I wondered whether he was doing what he did with respect to beet sugar in this country because he wanted to help his friends or because these interests were so powerful that he did not dare do otherwise.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: On a point of order, my hon. friend is suggesting that the Liberal party has entered into an agreement with persons unknown not to extend the sugar industry. I would point out to him that there 'has been more expansion of the sugar industry in the last five years than in any other five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: On a point of order, I also wish to point out to the hon. member that under section 158 of the criminal code, if he is making allegations of this kind he should proceed in the customary fashion, according to that section of the code; otherwise he has said too much or too little.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: Yes; I know the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) is a champion bluffer, but he does not bluff me, and I am perfectly aware of the protection I have in this house. I would point out to the hon. member that a man, in order to attack interests so powerful as the ones I am trying to move, needs all the protection he can get because they, the interests, have plenty of it.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
I am not so much concerned with the remarks the hon. member

Beet Sugar Industry
made against the government, but I did think he stated that the Prime Minister was responsible for this reprehensible practice.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
I think you will find, Mr. Speaker, that the record will show that
is not the case.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: If the hon. member tells me that I am wrong in my impression I will take his word, but that was what I understood him to say.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
I am endeavouring to speak loudly enough so that Your Honour will hear, but perhaps it is difficult at that. I did not say anything to reflect on the Prime Minister's honour.
Now I will deal shortly with the remarks of the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe). Suppose the industry has expanded; it has not expanded in my area to any great extent. I have some other things which it would do the Liberals good to contemplate.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: They will have a lot of time to do it after the next election.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: I suggest that it has expanded in the hon. gentleman's area in the last few years.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: We shall leave the records to show it.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: One of the last jobs I did was to design the extension of that plant.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
It would be nearly impossible to sell her much shorter than the Liberals have done already; she is short of nearly everything. What happened in Canada? I have in my hand a statement issued by the wartime prices and trade board on May 2, 1940, in reply to a statement given to the press on May 1, 1940, by the chairman of a committee representing the Southern Alberta Beet Growers association; this will be found in the Ottawa Citizen of May 2, 1940:
At the conclusion of the interview the chairman1-
That is the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board.
-stated explicitly to the delegation that the '[DOT]wartime prices and trade board, as a federal authority, was not in a position to do anything whatsoever to assist the expansion of the sugar beet industry in Canada."
And further on:
"At no time was any suggestion made," said the chairman, "that the wartime prices and trade board would proceed either directly or indirectly to encourage the expansion of the beet sugar industry."
Oh, what immaculate honour! At that time was not Hitler's power apparent? Had not most of the nations of western Europe fallen? Had not people everywhere awakened from their idiotic dream that Hitler would not last? Then why could nothing be done to assist in preparing this country against the dangers that yet lay ahead?
But we have not yet reached the climax. In the spring of 1941 word came out from Canadian Sugar Factories Limited-page the Minister of Munitions and Supply!-at Raymond that 1,300 acres of beets must be taken out of cultivation that year. In that area 1,300 acres of beets under normal conditions would produce 5,569,200 pounds of sugar. The reason given by the factories was that they had 200,000 hundredweight of sugar in their warehouses which they could not sell. Who was at fault because they were unable to sell? Let me read a statement from order in council P.C. 1983 dated May 15, 1940, setting forth the powers of the sugar controller. Hon. members will notice that he started his work in May of 1940, while the incident to which I have been referring took place in 1941, so that he had had time to find his way around. These are the words:
All sugar refiners in Canada shall sell to the sugar administrator as and when required by him, all raw sugar, and all refined sugar, syrups, liquid sugar and molasses manufactured from beets or cane now or hereafter in their possession at such prices as the sugar administrator, under the direction of the wartime
Beet Sugar Industry

prices and trade board, from time to time may prescribe and, to effectuate suoh power, the sugar administrator, under the direction of the board, shall have power to take possession of all or any such sugars accordingly.
Who appointed the sugar administrator? The Liberal party. At whose instigation? Well, you tell me. Whose business was he doing when he would have allowed these 1,300 acres to be taken out of cultivation? Let someone supply the answer; I have been trying to find out. Certainly he was not looking after the welfare of the people of Canada. Undoubtedly it was that man's fault that 200,000 hundredweight of sugar remained unsold in the storehouses of these factories. Whose fault was it that 1,300 acres were to be taken out of cultivation? It was the fault of no one but the sugar controller. Whoever appointed him, whoever instigated his appointment, was responsible for the decision to take that land out of cultivation. Fortunately, because of the pressure of public opinion, the unwise decision was rescinded and the 1,300 acres were put back into cultivation. Let us remember that this was in 1941. In those days there was no doubt about the terrific power of the enemy we were fighting; yet there were men in this country who could toy with an industry upon which the very lives of the people depended. For whose benefit? Well, we are all trying to find out. I suggested an answer.
Then we had rationing, and now we have scarcity. I am going to call upon the Toronto Globe and Mail to consider the array of evidence which I have submitted, and I wish to ask them to take a little time off to explain, in the light of that evidence, how they justify themselves in characterizing my remarks as irresponsible utterances. Someone in this parliament, Mr. Chairman, must rise and defend the cause of the common man; but he who stands in this House of Commons and undertakes to battle for the truth finds all the terrible powers of this country dead against him, and that he must labour under every handicap. Then, if he endeavours to use the rules as a means of strengthening himself, he must be abused by what should be a responsible newspaper and by those who should be responsible men. It does not hurt me; I came here to defend the cause of the common man and I am going to defend it. Now I invite the Prime Minister and the Toronto Globe and Mail to spend any necessary amount of time to prepare a satisfying explanation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: You would not have them together?

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: No; they had better work separately, though apparently they did not do so in the last instance; the one copied from the other. Let them prepare an explanation that will satisfy any hard-headed, common-sense man, an explanation that will justify the government in following the questionable policy with respect to sugar which has prevailed in this country. I shall be told, as one of the stock reasons why it is necessary to avoid any expansion of the beet sugar industry during wartime, that we must not have too much beet sugar producing capacity at the end of the war because we have to sell abroad and therefore we must buy abroad. That is the stock argument, May I ask those who would bring forward such a foolish argument if we ought to stop manufacturing agricultural machinery in Canada in order that we might buy from Britain or Germany. Should we stop manufacturing shoes and clothing in Canada in order that we might buy from the United States, in order that we might sell our wheat? Should we stop manufacturing lumber in order that we might trade with Russia, or stop manufacturing cheese and butter in order that we might trade with our sister dominion, New Zealand? Those sound like intelligent proposals, do they not? Or should we stop producing oil in order that we might trade with Roumania?

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: That is one thing of which we are producing very little in Canada,

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: But should we stop even that little production? Well, if we would not stop producing these commodities we have mentioned, why stop producing sugar from beets?

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: WThen did we stop?

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: When limiting production.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: When did we do that?

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
In 1941, and ever since the signing of or the acquiescence in the international trade agreement, as I have abundantly proved. I think the minister will find, when he reads my remarks in Hansard, that it will be hard to find an answer to them.
Some will say: "Is the sugar from the beets as good?" Yes, it is exactly the same kind of sugar. It is the same, chemically, as sugar wherever you find it, or whatever it is made from.
Then they will say: "Is it cheap enough?" I point out only this fact, that according to the report which I have here from Canadian Sugar Factories Limited, for 1938-and I am speaking

Beet Sugar Industry
from memory, although I am sure I have it right-they sold their sugar for a net price of $3.94 a hundredweight in. 1937.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: F.O.B. mill?

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: That is the year they made $155, to which I refer. I say that $3.94 a hundredweight is pretty cheap sugar.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: At what point?

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: At the refinery. All this manoeuvring of the Liberal party in connection with the restriction of the production of beet sugar I think we must characterize as the most effective government cooperation with somebody-and if not the sugar interests, then with whom?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: There has never been any restriction of the production of beet sugar.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
There has been an expansion
in every year of the war.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
Some men looking at sunlight in broad day would declare it was dark. This is cooperation with these interests in what appears to be an international conspiracy to impose either scarcity or high prices or both upon the people of Canada, through an agreement on Canada's part to refuse to assist in any way the expansion of the beet sugar industry in Canada-the beet sugar industry, for which Canada is extraordinarily well adapted. I see no way in which one can explain that in any other way.
Now, another serious thing: This participation, in the international sugar agreement appears to be not only a conspiracy to foist high prices upon the Canadian people but, perhaps worse still, and yet more sinister, it appears also to be an agreement, or complacency, or conscious if not wilful acquiescence on the part of the King government, in an international plan to rob Canada of her economic independence.
Sugar is one of the most vital needs of the Canadian people. In fact it is practically indispensable to them. Imagine how helpless might be the condition of the Canadian people if an international organization, desiring to brow-beat Canada into some policy repugnant to Canadians were to threaten to withhold from Canada the sugar her people needs! In such a condition the threat of withholding sugar would be a fearful weapon, through the use of which an international organization could destroy Canada's independence. It would be a weapon even more potent than an international police force. I repeat: it looks as though the King government had been at least cooperating with interests definitely aiming at the destruction of Canada's sovereignty.
There are some who smile. I will tell you that if some of the schemes which these supranational government artists are trying to have fixed on this country succeed, the smile will be on the other side of the face. This method of food control is exactly the strategy and technique by which they seem to intend to work.
Let the people of Canada know, and I hereby declare to them that, except for the opposition of the sugar interests and the government's acquiescence in that opposition, the domestic production of sugar in Canada could now be meeting the domestic non-rationed requirements not only of Canada but of a very considerable portion of the English-speaking world. Let me give the house just a few figures to indicate the truth of what I say. The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) in his brief points out that the county of Lambton alone could produce twenty five per cent of all Canada's sugar needs in peacetime. They could support four factories of 1,200-ton slicing capacity. And he points out that Kent, Essex, Middlesex and Huron are all counties admirably adapted to the production of sugar beets, and that they could produce the sugar which Canada requires. Why is that not being done?
Now, in Doctor Archibald's report, to which I referred earlier, with respect to the Alberta sugar beet situation, published on October 2S, 1937, he points out that only 20,000 acres were being used in Alberta for the production of sugar beets, and that 200,000 acres of irrigated land of just as fine quality were available for sugar beet production in that province. May I point out that in my constituency by the expenditure of $15,000,000 in the construction of the Lethbridge south-east water conservation project 350,000 more acres of as fine quality as are now producing sugar beets could be brought into cultivation. There is no doubt in the world that Canada can produce all the sugar she needs.
I turn now to the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount. I wish I had time to deal with his speech categorically, but I shall be able to make only a few comments with respect to it. As for his contribution to the debate I would say that as one who comes from the citadel of high finance the faults in his argument can be explained. Any man who undertakes to talk about matters concerning which he has little information and less understanding will naturally blunder at every turn, as did the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: What is the hon. member reading from?

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
Does the hon. member wish me to read the article?



Beet Sugar Industry

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: I am glad to see he has committed it to writing.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
I am referring to the speech which he delivered, with respect to my speech. Of course he thought my remarks were full of inconsistencies. It requires a well-informed man to follow the reasoning of another well-informed man. The hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount appears to argue that even if Canada had been committed to beet sugar industry of no matter how great an extent, her domestic sugar production could have made no difference to the quantity of supplies available for wartime consumption in Canada.
Suppose, Mr. Speaker, that Canada had thirty sugar factories of 1,200-ton slicing capacity, which she could easily have in Alberta and Ontario alone, and producing one and a half times the amount of sugar she needs, are we to be told in all seriousness that that production would make no difference to the sugar which the Canadian people would have? If that is the case, then I ask what foolhardy policy it was that dictated the signing of an agreement which rendered such a thing as that possible?

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: The hon. member left out Manitoba in his list of provinces which could produce beet sugar. They are growing sugar beets out there, and also have a sugar beet factory.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
I knew that the Manitoba people would not mind. The point I wished to make was that two provinces alone in Canada could produce one and a half times the sugar we need. And if you bring in the other provinces there is no reason in the world why this country should be without sugar. This thing of trying to argue the Canadian people into the idea that it is the war which brought on the shortage of sugar is simply deluding the people. There must be a complete change in the whole outlook in respect of many commodities produced in this country. We must stop the restricted, short-sighted, narrow-minded point of view, or using the point of view we have had up to the present time. We must reach out in a generous way, we must use the resources of our country and distribute them so that the Canadian people may have abundance.
In closing, I again make an offer to anyone in the Liberal party who thinks he can explain away the arguments I have advanced, and upon which I base my suspicion that secret influence has been brought to bear upon the government to bring about a policy of restriction with respect to the production of beet sugar in Canada since the beginning of the

war; to attempt to do so. I have not said anything about prices, although I mentioned prices in my speech. I have an array of figures which would be quite as impressive, and perhaps if the opportunity offers at some time I shall give particulars of the prices to indicate that there has been manipulation resulting in the Canadian people having to pay more for their sugar than they should have had to pay.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not very anxious to get into this debate, but several references have been made to the party, of which I happen to be a member. There are at present in the house four members who were members of the agriculture committee which sat in 1932. The hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) was the chairman; the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) was a member, as well as the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) and myself. The question of encouraging the production of sugar from beets in Canada was referred to that committee. I have before me the report of the committee which was presented to the house on April 1, 1932, and I should like to read one or two paragraphs from the report, as follows:
The evidence submitted established the following facts regarding the industry:
1.	That the production of sugar beets has been carried on very profitably in certain districts of Ontario and Alberta; that the area under cultivation has increased from 25,000 acres in 1921 with a yield of 200,000 tons to 42,000 acres in 1931, with a yield of approximately 435,000 tons, and that the production of refined beet sugar has increased from 53,000.000 pounds in 1921 to approximately 100,000,000 pounds in 1931.
That is in ten years. The report goes on:
2.	That large additional areas, suitable for the growth of sugar beets, are available in Canada.
And again:
5. That the sugar beet factories at Chatham, Wallaceburg and Raymond are now operating at full capacity, and that no further development of the beet sugar industry in Canada is possible until manufacturing capacity is increased.
The final paragraphs of the report read:
Your committee therefore recommends that in view of the existing tariff on sugar and in consideration of the substantial payments being made to agriculture and labour by the beet sugar factories at present in operation, the cane sugar refineries should undertake to provide for a gradual increase in factory facilities for the refining of beet sugar in Canada, and that, with the additional advantages in freight rates to points in the middle west, heretofore described, factory facilities should now be steadily increased in western areas where beets are grown, and thereby make it possible to produce from beets a more substantial percentage of the sugar consumption of Canada.

War Expenditures Committee
Your committee further recommends, that if no successful attempt ibe made in the immediate future by the refineries to increase the facilities for the manufacture of beet sugar, the government should take into consideration steps to accomplish that end.
I read from that report to show that the government of that day and the agriculture committee of that day were ready to encourage the production of beet sugar in Canada. Since that time there has been a considerable increase in the production of beet sugar in Manitoba. There is a splendid refinery located there and I suggest to all hon. members that they visit it. It is one of the best in Canada and it has great possibilities. I say these few words to show that the party of that day was interested in increasing the beet sugar industry of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the sugar agreement of 1938 was wholly to increase the supplies of sugar and to divide them equally among the people who were preparing for war. During every one. of the last five or six years there has. been an expansion in the sugar beet industry. The sugar beet refinery in Winnipeg which was referred to was,completed'within the last three or four years, and recently a new industry has been started in Quebec. I can assure my hon. friend that if any other interest wishes to increase the production of beet sugar in any area of this country they will have the support of the government, as has every -other beet sugar project that has come along.
In connection with the project in Quebec there was an acute shortage of building materials, and it was difficult to justify the use of the materials for that purpose when -they were needed for direct war projects. Nevertheless the government decided that the project was of such importance that an exception must be made and the beet sugar plant in Quebec was classed as a war project.
I can say categorically that this government has taken no action that would in any way limit the production of sugar in Canada. I can give evidence of the fact that we have given every assistance to those interests that wished to expand the production of beet sugar in this country.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: How about the 1,300 acres in 1941?	-

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: That is absolute nonsense.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: It is not nonsense. My hon. friend has just forgotten, that'is all; he does not know.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: What about the old and well established, sugar refinery in Halifax which was closed down recently because of war conditions. The conditions that forced the closing of that refinery have pretty well rectified themselves. Cane sugar is now coming into Halifax harbour and going to other parts of Canada. Can the minister give the house any information as to when the Acadia sugar refinery will reopen and again be producing sugar?

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: The house is not in committee. My hon. friend is standing up for the sugar barons who use cane sugar. I may say that no action of the government closed the refinery in Halifax. It is my understanding that it was bought by private interests who decided that it was better closed than open.

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: The government had no authority to keep it open?

maintopic: DEET SUGAR INDUSTRY IN CANADA- STATEMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
The government has plenty of
authority.

maintopic: WAR EXPENDITURES COMMITTEE-IN CAMERA SITTINGS-MR. HOMUTH

speechtext: Mr. KARL K. HOMUTH (Waterloo South): Mr. Speaker, now that we have finished a sweet subject, perhaps I may be pardoned for interjecting something sour into the debate. I do this because I feel the matter I have in mind is of considerable public importance and is directly associated with the activities of the Department of Munitions and Supply. I know of no other time to take up this matter than on the motion to go into supply. I refer to the matter of whether the war expenditures committee should sit in camera or in public and to the question which I had with Mr. Speaker with regard to it.

maintopic: WAR EXPENDITURES COMMITTEE-IN CAMERA SITTINGS-MR. HOMUTH
speechtext:
I think the hon. member has given me sufficient indication of what he intends to speak on. He is proposing to deal with an opinion which I gave to him personally regarding the secrecy of the meetings of the war expenditures committee and I must rule that on the motion to go into supply the hon. member cannot discuss that matter. The rule is perfectly clear according to citation 568 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition, which reads as follows:
Until the report' and evidence have been laid upon the table, it is irregular to refer to them in debate, or to put questions in reference to the proceedings of the committee.
The reference is to select committees. That rule is also borne out by Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure, at page 474, wherein it is stated:	.
Until a committee report, it is irregular to refer to its proceedings in debate in the house.
Deserter at Longueuil

For instance, in. the session of 1873, Mr. Huntington was proceeding to refer to certain papers and letters relative to an important matter under the consideration of a select committee; but the speaker decided in accordance with English precedents that they could not be read in the house (a). Neither can a committee report the evidence taken before a similar committee in a previous session. . . .
The matter that the hon. member has referred to is a matter under discussion in the committee. It is not before the house. It is not a grievance in the sense that the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) spoke of this evening. It is a matter purely of proceeding, which is within the hands of the committee. It is not before the house and therefore I must rule that the hon. member cannot bring it up.

maintopic: WAR EXPENDITURES COMMITTEE-IN CAMERA SITTINGS-MR. HOMUTH
speechtext:
But is a grievance. It is one of those grievances that we cannot bring before the house and the hon. members are stymied.
Mr. SPEAKER; The hon. member will have opportunities in the proceedings of the house but I cannot now indicate them. At the moment we are on. the motion to go into supply. It is not a grievance in the sense that is intended when the committee of supply is being set up. As I have already said, it is a matter that is before the committee. It is a proceeding which they are dealing with. It is a matt ;r which cannot be brought before the house in the manner in which the hon. member is now trying.

maintopic: WAR EXPENDITURES COMMITTEE-IN CAMERA SITTINGS-MR. HOMUTH
speechtext: May I crave Your Honour's indulgence for a word in this matter?

maintopic: WAR EXPENDITURES COMMITTEE-IN CAMERA SITTINGS-MR. HOMUTH
speechtext:
I am always ready to listen to the leader of the opposition, but in this instance my position is perfectly clear. I have no doubt'in my mind as to the soundness of the rule I am now propounding and it r-ust be taken without argument.
Mr. GRAYDON; I am sorry Your Honour made that ruling because this is the situation in which we find ourselves. The committee has ruled in a certain direction.. We have an appeal to. Your Honour but we are not allowed to exercise that appeal. In a few words, that is what it means.

maintopic: WAR EXPENDITURES COMMITTEE-IN CAMERA SITTINGS-MR. HOMUTH

At the moment there is, in my judgment, nothing before the Chair which would justify the hon. member in bringing up this question when going into supply.

He can never bring it up

maintopic: CASE OF DESERTER AT LONGUEUIL-MR. POULIOT

speechtext:
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, in accordance with your ruling I shall not speak about that matter. I wonder if the leader of the opposition has something more to say. I have another case that I shall bring to the attention of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). I shall summarize in a few words what it is. There was a fellow who. deserted for about a month or two. He was sentenced to the clink in Longueuil, and I am informed that he suffers from sinus trouble. The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) told me that I could have a copy of his examination with a letter from the man authorizing the department to give it to me. I sent a draft letter of two or three lines to his brother and asked him to go to Longueuil and have it signed by the man. The brother could not see him that day, and then I wrote a letter to the man with that draft letter of two or three lines. The letter was along these lines:
I hereby authorize the department to give a copy of my medical examination to J. F. Pouliot.
That letter was registered. The command1-ing officer said to that man:
If you sign that letter you will be punished for that or if you send that letter.
I am informed that the letter has been signed, has been sent to me and has been held by the officer because I have not received it. Since that time the man has been condemned to bread and water and the restrictions upon him have been more severe. Naturally I do not blame headquarters for that treatment, but there is something wrong there. That man had a most unsatisfactory medical examination. In Longueuil a young man who had heart trouble was ordered* to shovel sand in a cart for a whole day. There is something wrong there. I shall ask the minister kindly to send someone from Ottawa, someone who has nothing to do with the garrison at Longueuil and have a report made on that case. It seems to be a reasonable request to make. If the situation is as I am informed it is, it reminds me of* the dark ages of long ago. That man cannot be treated like that. I have a right to his examination, upon the conditions set by the parliamentary assistant to the minister. He said to me:
Let us have a letter from that man.; let us be authorized by that man and I shall give you a copy of the examination.

German Prisoners in Canada
That man cannot write me. The medical doctors of the army at Longueuil have already, to my knowledge, freed some men. When I complain of this case I know whereof I speak. I know also that these men have been freed after I directed the attention of headquarters to the case. It is time it should finish; whoever is in charge in Longueoiil should be severely punished if the facts that I have given are true, and I presume they are because up until how they have been.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: CASE OF DESERTER AT LONGUEUIL-MR. POULIOT
speechtext:
I want to say to my hon. friend
that I have the greatest confidence in the officer who is in charge at Longueuil. I shall be very glad to look into the matter to which he has referred. As he has said himself, it is not a matter for headquarters, but a matter of administration in the district. I shall have an examination made. If he had referred the matter to me I can assure him I would have been very glad to have had it looked into without taking up the time of the house.

maintopic: TREATMENT OF GERMAN PRISONERS OF WAR IN CANADA-MR. ROSS (SOURIS)
TREATMENT OF GERMAN PRISONERS OF WAR IN CANADA-MR. ROSS (SOURIS)
speechtext:
On this occasion I should like to raise a question in regard to enemy prisoners in this country. It is not only to-day that the press has carried stories across the country with regard to German prisoners, but on other occasions in my province that has happened for some months past now. To-day the press has carried a report concerning hun prisoners being given free rein at Buckingham. The press states that they drink in taverns and go out with local girls. The ire of townspeople is aroused. This is a quotation from a local paper:
The prisoners allegedly getting this favoured treatment are engaged in. work for the Singer Company in timber limits near Thurso.
The article points out that these prisoners had been taken into Buckingham for dental treatment, I think, by a guard. Following that, the guard took them to the tavern where they drank beer freely. Then he took them in an automobile, and they went to some other place and picked up the other guard along with four girls or young ladies and went carousing around the country that evening. It is quite a lengthy article and it points out ihe disgust of those people, the relatives of young people serving in the armed services. Certainly it is not a very nice situation. There is a lengthy article which may be found in various papers to-day. The minister will find it there. As I say, had this been the only
case I would not have raised the issue right now, but in the Dauphin Herald, of Manitoba of February 24 there was a very strong protest, as follows:
For the second time within two months a German officer from the prison camp on the Riding Mountain has been seen on the streets of Dauphin under very loose courtesy custody.
Doctor and professional man though he may be, he is still a captive German and must be regarded as an enemy of the country.
Shortly before Christmas this same officer was taken in broad daylight and with a full view of everything right into No. 10 service flying training school, R.C.A.F., at Dauphin. The excuse then was that he had to accompany another German prisoner to the air school to have his teeth fixed.
_ On the same occasion the enemy officer asked if he might visit the medical clinic at Dauphin and permission was readily accorded by the pliant guard.
In the name of the parents of this country whose boys at this very moment are fighting for their lives in Italy we protest against this preferred treatment and we warn the Department of National Defence, that the next time we see this German prisoner on the streets of Dauphin we shall proclaim the fact in three-inch head-fines and send a copy to every newspaper in Canada.
This is a war to the death we are now engaged in as many of us already know to our sorrow.
That will indicate that this practice has been prevalent, apparently, in these camps. We have a report to-day from this town in Quebec and these other reports from the area in my native province to the west.	*
The minister during his own war appropriation bill rather took me to task when I asked a question about recruiting at this time. He said he thought he was getting splendid results following these recruiting parties and dances being held throughout the country. Well, that is going on, on the one hand, and this laxity on the other, and it does not create a very good feeling among the parents and relatives of the boys who are serving overseas to-day. It is a very bad situation.
I maintain that we have not to this day national selective service in operation as we should have for the armed services, for agriculture and for industry. Anybody knows that the system of recruiting to-day is far from satisfactory.

maintopic: TREATMENT OF GERMAN PRISONERS OF WAR IN CANADA-MR. ROSS (SOURIS)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, is this a grievance or is this anything which can be discussed on this motion? 1 am rising to a point of order. My hon. friend may have been within his rights in discussing German prisoners of war, but I submit he is not within his rights in discussing what has already been discussed on the war appropriation resolution, which was before the committee for three weeks: I myself was here at that time for a
German Prisoners in Canada

week. I made my answer to my hon. friend. He could answer or not just as he liked. But I say that he cannot take the opportunity now, on a motion to go into supply, to raise >
matter which has already been discussed on what in effect were estimates under the war appropriation resolution.

maintopic: TREATMENT OF GERMAN PRISONERS OF WAR IN CANADA-MR. ROSS (SOURIS)
speechtext:
I shall not deal any further with that phase of the matter. Had I been able to raise the question on the orders of the day I would have preferred to have done it at that time, but I realize how far I could have gone on the orders of the day in this matter.
To many thousands of relatives of our men throughout the country this will appear a very serious situation. To permit such unreasonable conduct by enemy prisoners in our midst is an insult to the relatives of those who are serving overseas to-day on our behalf. The present camp in Riding Mountain was built last fall under a wartime housing scheme. I personally visited it upon its completion, and I say that it is the most up-to-date camp I have ever been in. There are conveniences and comforts there which very few of the pioneers of this country are able to afford to-day. I think our prisoners should have proper treatment, but they should be properly guarded, and insults such as have been allowed in the last few days and few months should not be tolerated in this country. I cannot think of anything more insulting to the relatives of the boys in the armed services. A statement from the responsible minister with regard to this very serious and nasty occurrence is due to this house and to the citizens of Canada.

maintopic: TREATMENT OF GERMAN PRISONERS OF WAR IN CANADA-MR. ROSS (SOURIS)
speechtext:
Before the minister replies I should like to odd a word to what has been said by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) regarding the treatment of German prisoners in Canada. Hon. members will recall that last session the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) ^ead a statement in the house regarding the treatment accorded to British and Canadian prisoners held by the Japanese. It was a copy of the statement given in the British House of Commons by Mr. Anthony Eden. Hon. members will recall that almost unheard-of savage and barbarian treatment inflicted by the Japanese on British and Canadian soldiers. I am vitally interested in Ihese Canadian boys because fifty-two of the soldiers from the district in which I reside were at Hong Kong and are now prisoners of the Japanese. I wonder what the parents and the families of the boys who are now in Japanese hands must think when they hear over the radio and read in the press to-day of
[Mr. Ralston.!
the de luxe treatment accorded to German prisoners in this country. If any hon. members took the trouble to read the article which appeared in the February 7 issue of the United States magazine Lije, they will recall the very full statements by American officers and men who escaped from the Japanese in which they give firsthand, accurate information as to the manner in which their prisoners are treated.
I protest strongly against the fashion in which these German prisoners are treated in Canada. The hon. member for Souris says it is an insult. To me "insult" is not an adequate description of the feelings of the parents and beloved ones of Canadian boys who languish in Japanese prison camps when they read of the way we are treating German prisoners in this country. I concur in everything the hon. member for Souris has said, and I think it is the minister's duty to make a very full statement on this matter.

maintopic: TREATMENT OF GERMAN PRISONERS OF WAR IN CANADA-MR. ROSS (SOURIS)
speechtext:
I do not know how many times I am allowed to take part in this debate. I have already spoken once. But I am not going to let the remarks which have been made by hon. members to pass unless you, Mr. Speaker, consider that I am not in order in discussing them.
In regard to the Thurso incident, I, like my hon. friends, first saw it in this evening's papers. My hon. friend does not suppose that I have a personal check on these matters or know all that is going on. But I immediately called up the adjutant general to find out what he knew about it, and I was informed that he was getting a report on the matter and that, as a matter of fact, the director of prisoners of war had already sent someone to Thurso to ascertain what the situation was.
Let me say first of all that, with regard to this matter of prisoners of war in working camps, I warned this house last session that we were having great pressure to allow prisoners of war to work, and I told the house that so far as the Department of National Defence was concerned, we must point out that there were some risks involved, because we could not exercise strict supervision when they were outside the internment camps. We felt, however, in view of the strong pressure which was being brought to bear, that we should do the very best we could to make prisoners of war available for work.
We have not a veteran's guard sufficiently numerous to guard all these prisoners; that is to say, to accompany the individuals. They have to have some leeway. But they are working in camps at the insistence of the public of this country, and I warned them that a certain number of these prisoners would pro-

German Prisoners in Canada
bably escape. The house seemed to take it as quite all right so long as that labour was provided.
At Thurso, as I understand from the very little I have .learned, these men came down to have some dentistry done. There was a corporal with them. I do not want to misjudge his case. I may say that as a result of the incident he is under close arrest. Apparently there were some irregularities, and the irregularities will be looked into. While it is not something which occurs every day, these things do happen from time to time. However, the matter will be gone into thoroughly.
I wish to point out to my hon. friends that when prisoners of war are sent outside the internment camps to do work it is not possible to have a guard for each one of them. When they are brought to a centre they are brought in as small numbers as possible, and it is thought that the guard provided is sufficient under the circumstances. We cannot possibly send guards to the lumber woods to guard these prisoners of war to the extent of having a guard for each prisoner, and the result, therefore, sometimes is that these irregularities take place. But the matter will be investigated and whatever disciplinary action is necessary will be taken.
WTth regard to the Dauphin case, I never heard of it before. That was the case of a prisoner of wTar working in one of the labour camps, not in one of the internment camps.
As regards prisoners in internment camps my hon. friend will not have much to complain about. They are dealt with under close guard, and I think the public have reason to be pretty well satsified with the way in which the internment camps have been conducted in this country, considering the number of men we have and the fact that these men from day to day have nothing to do but to sit and plan how to escape. I pay tribute to the veterans' guard of Canada for the splendid way in which they have carried on in seeing that these >
prisoners are properly guarded.

maintopic: TREATMENT OF GERMAN PRISONERS OF WAR IN CANADA-MR. ROSS (SOURIS)
speechtext: So do I.

maintopic: TREATMENT OF GERMAN PRISONERS OF WAR IN CANADA-MR. ROSS (SOURIS)
speechtext:
The record cannot be excelled anywhere of the way in which they have been handled.
Coming back to prisoners like the one in the Dauphin case -who are working, there is a different situation existing there and there cannot be the same strict and complete supervision. There are not the same number of guards provided. I have an arrangement with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) whereby we are responsible for guards up to a certain point, and after that my hon. friend takes
over. We supply a nucleus to help with the discipline in the labour camp, but as regards security generally the responsibility is that of the Department of Labour. Having regard to all they have to do in that respect, they have done an excellent job and have provided a great many prisoners of war to do work. They have done a great deal of work with little trouble to the citizens.
With regard to the treatment of prisoners of war, I do not know what either of my hon. friends is talking about when he speaks of de luxe treatment. They are treated in accordance with the Geneva convention, and regardless of what some barbarous nation does as regards prisoners of war, so far as I am concerned, prisoners of war will be treated according to the terms of that convention, and we will live up to it. From, the point of view of the citizens of Canada, their boys are either in Hong Kong or in German prison camps and if we treated prisoners of war here contrary to the terms of that convention, their mothers and fathers here would be the first to say, and say rightly, that the Dominion of Canada, through the Department of National Defence, had brought on their boys in the prison camps of Germany and Japan persecution and hardship by reason of the fact that we treated German or Japanese prisoners of war improperly here. I have seen the representative of the protecting power and have had him go over all the camps and report to me personally to see that they were living up to the terms of the Geneva convention, and I assure this house that nothing more than that is done, I propose to follow that policy straight through so long as the Department of National Defence has the responsibility.
The house can see that we are in a difficult situation. We do not want to treat them better than we are required to do according to the letter of the law. At the same time, however, reports do get back, and if anything goes wrong reports will immediately reach the powers detaining our boys, with the result that hardships are imposed on them and then the families in this country feel that the action we have taken against German prisoners has been visited upon their boys overseas. We have to hew to the line and that is what we are endeavouring to do.
I assure hon. members that if there is any case in which the line is overstepped I do not know of it. I shall look into the case of Thurso. That is a case where apparently some men got liquor and perhaps those in charge engaged in irregularities. Disciplinary action will be taken. The Dauphin case I will look into. I understand from my hon. friend that somebody wanted the attention of
German Prisoners in Canada

a dental officer and went to an air force camp in order to get it. I do not see anything wrong about that at first blush, though there may be. I will say that they were not in the custody of the Department of National Defence at the time but in a labour camp, which is authorized by the government and the house, and which has been urged by the people of the country in order that they may get the advantage of the prisoner of wa-labour available for that purpose.
I have nothing more to say except that I shall look into both cases, and if there is any cause for complaint I assure the house it will be rectified.

maintopic: TREATMENT OF GERMAN PRISONERS OF WAR IN CANADA-MR. ROSS (SOURIS)
speechtext: After the investigation, will the minister tell the house what the regulations are with respect to taking these prisoners into centres of population?

maintopic: TREATMENT OF GERMAN PRISONERS OF WAR IN CANADA-MR. ROSS (SOURIS)
speechtext: I do not know that there are any regulations particularly. Both these cases, I believe, as a matter of fact were men from labour camps and not from internment camps. The Minister of Labour will tell the hon. gentleman if there are special regulations about them. I have no doubt they are taken to centres of population when it is necessary to take them for treatment. The only question is as to the adequacy of the guard provided for that purpose.

maintopic: TREATMENT OF GERMAN PRISONERS OF WAR IN CANADA-MR. ROSS (SOURIS)
speechtext:
In view of the fact that my department is probably involved, I should like to say a few words. I had not known anything about the matter. The first I knew about it was what I found in the newspapers this evening; in fact I had not read it until my hon. friend mentioned it.
There is nothing novel about the employment of prisoners of war outside internment camps.

maintopic: TREATMENT OF GERMAN PRISONERS OF WAR IN CANADA-MR. ROSS (SOURIS)
speechtext: I am not objecting to that.

maintopic: TREATMENT OF GERMAN PRISONERS OF WAR IN CANADA-MR. ROSS (SOURIS)
speechtext:
Many members have
approached me in an effort to get prisoners of war to work on farms and in other industries in the country in view of the severe manpower situation. In South Africa there are 60,000 prisoners of war working outside internment camps. They have them in Great Britain and in the United States and it is a question of man-power. As the Minister of National Defence has said, if you have to have as many guards as you have prisoners, you might as well use the guards and not bother about the prisoners. May I say to the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White) that I do not think the Anglo-Saxons have reached the level where we should endeavour to match brutality with brutality.

maintopic: TREATMENT OF GERMAN PRISONERS OF WAR IN CANADA-MR. ROSS (SOURIS)
speechtext: I never suggested that we should match the Japanese at all, but I do not think we should adopt a continual appeasement policy.

maintopic: TREATMENT OF GERMAN PRISONERS OF WAR IN CANADA-MR. ROSS (SOURIS)
speechtext:
There is no appeasement about it, but I say this to my hon. friend. As long as I am in charge of prisoners of war I am going to maintain that same dignity of treatment afforded human beings which has made the British people what they are. I know it is the easiest thing in the world, to raise this kind of question, to set passions aflame, and no one regrets more than I do the treatment of prisoners of war in Japan. But I think this will readily be understood, that after all, in that part of the world, they have just a veneer of civilization and that is all. It would not, however, redound to our credit if we varied in any detail from the international law laid down in the Geneva convention for the treatment of prisoners of war in this country.
I join with the Minister of National Defence in the assurance that we will look into the matter. I am frank to admit that in the employment of prisoners of war some risk is run. We often read in the newspapers that our young fellows manage to escape from Germany and other parts of the continent, and that is one of the inevitable risks which those people who desire such assistance at this time, in the way of man-power, have to take. It has to be taken in every country where prisoners of war are employed outside the regular internment camps. I would go so far as to say that there have been actually more escapes from internment camps in this country than there have been from what we might call the work camps under the jurisdiction of my department.
I shall be glad to look into the matter as far as it affects my department and give my hon. friend the information he desires.

maintopic: INCOME TAX-POSSIBILITY OF EXTENSION OF TIME FOR FINAL PAYMENT-MR. KNOWLES

speakeroldname: Mr. S. H. KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre):
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: INCOME TAX-POSSIBILITY OF EXTENSION OF TIME FOR FINAL PAYMENT-MR. KNOWLES
speechtext:
There is another matter I should like to bring to the attention of the government before Your Honour leaves the Chair. It is a matter about which questions have been asked, but as yet hon. members have had no opportunity to discuss it or to express the views of their constituents. I refer to the problem created for a great many people by the necessity of paying the entire balance due on their 1943 income tax by April 30. As I say, questions have been asked in the house about this matter, and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson) in reply has simply stated the terms of the statute as it stands.

Income Tax
As hon. members are aware, it is a matter of considerable urgency for a great many people. We hope the government may give some consideration to this matter, and that such consideration might be given soon, so that if any change in policy is to be made an announcement to that effect might be given at an early date. Following many letters which I have received on this matter, I wrote the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) -

maintopic: INCOME TAX-POSSIBILITY OF EXTENSION OF TIME FOR FINAL PAYMENT-MR. KNOWLES
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, surely this does not come within the rules on going into supply. The hon. member is talking about a matter which will not eventuate until April 30 of this year, and this is now only the middle of March.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: INCOME TAX-POSSIBILITY OF EXTENSION OF TIME FOR FINAL PAYMENT-MR. KNOWLES
speechtext: If I may speak to the point of order, in my reading of the rule with respect to the right of private members to raise grievances on going into supply I do not see anything about urgency. The rule refers to grievances: I submit that this is a grievance of my constitutents, and also that there is in it an element of urgency. The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) suggests that April 30 is a long way off. It really is not very far off when one considers the plans that people must make to take care, in many cases, of quite large sums that must be paid by way of balances of their income tax. I submit that it is in order, that it is a matter which should be brought to the attention of the government and a matter on which hon. members should have an opportunity to express their views at this time.

maintopic: INCOME TAX-POSSIBILITY OF EXTENSION OF TIME FOR FINAL PAYMENT-MR. KNOWLES
speechtext:
I would refer hon. members to citation 345 of Beauchesne's Rules and Forms:
The ancient doctrine that the redress of grievances should ibe considered before the grant of supplies is maintained in the House of Commons of Canada by the provision of standing order 49 that the motion for the Speaker to leave the chair can be amended; and the amendments need not be relevant but may relate to every question connected with public administration.
And further:
Matters of detail which should be discussed in committee cannot be debated on these occasions, nor can debate be permitted relating to grants already agreed to, or to resolutions which will be proposed in the committee, or to items in the estimates.
The other day I ruled that a matter which was being discussed could be taken up when the estimates were before the committee, but I know of no item, though I may be informed to the contrary, on which the matter to which the hon. member is now referring could be discussed. .

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: INCOME TAX-POSSIBILITY OF EXTENSION OF TIME FOR FINAL PAYMENT-MR. KNOWLES
speechtext: Item 189, covering the general administration of the income tax division.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: INCOME TAX-POSSIBILITY OF EXTENSION OF TIME FOR FINAL PAYMENT-MR. KNOWLES
speechtext: This is in reference to a statute passed last year, and no item covering it appears anywhere in this year's estimates.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: INCOME TAX-POSSIBILITY OF EXTENSION OF TIME FOR FINAL PAYMENT-MR. KNOWLES
speechtext: If I may interject a word, this collection of income tax comes about by virtue of a statute which has been on, the statute books for some twenty years, during which time income tax has been payable on April 30 of each year. One-third of the total had to be paid by April 30 and the remaining two-thirds, bearing an interest rate of five per cent, I think, must be paid by September 1. That has been the law. Last year an exception was made because of the change-over to the pay-as-you-go policy, but with that exception that date of April 30 has been fixed for some twenty years.

maintopic: INCOME TAX-POSSIBILITY OF EXTENSION OF TIME FOR FINAL PAYMENT-MR. KNOWLES
speechtext:
I am rather inclined to think the hon. member is in order. Item 189 reads:
Income tax division: general administration, including authority to create positions and make appointments-*
The matter being discussed by the hon. member has to do with the date of payment of the income tax, and I am rather inclined to believe that the hon. member is in order in discussing it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: INCOME TAX-POSSIBILITY OF EXTENSION OF TIME FOR FINAL PAYMENT-MR. KNOWLES
speechtext:
If I may continue, I believe I had referred to the fact that I wrote the Minister of Finance about this matter under date of March 9. He replied under date of March 11, and I should like to quote part of that letter:
As you know, the Minister of National Revenue stated in the house on Friday-
That would be on March 10, and that statement appears at page 1347 of Hansard.-.
-that no extension is at present contemplated. Your suggestion will, however, be kept in mind.
On the basis of that last short sentence, I felt there was some point in raising the matter in this way and pressing the government to give consideration to it, I was further encouraged by the reply given on the orders of the day to-day when the question was asked of the Minister of National Revenue; I felt that his answer at that time was not quite so final and categorical as the one he made on March 10. The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance has just made reference to the situation that has prevailed in years gone by, and has indicated that there has been no basic change. I should like to point out to him that there is considerable confusion

Labour Conditions

over this matter, and I should like also to call his attention to information that can be found by looking at the income tax form for various years. I have a number of them here in my hand. First I have the forms on which taxpayers are now working, the T-l special, 1943, $3,000 or under; and also T-l general, 1943. On each of these forms it is indicated that payment is to be made in full on April 30, and there is nothing anywhere in the form to indicate that any postponement or deferment is possible. If the house will permit me to move the adjournment of the debate, when I come back to the matter I shall refer, by way of contrast, to the information contained on the forms for 1942 and 1941.

maintopic: INCOME TAX-POSSIBILITY OF EXTENSION OF TIME FOR FINAL PAYMENT-MR. KNOWLES
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman moving the adjournment of the debate?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: INCOME TAX-POSSIBILITY OF EXTENSION OF TIME FOR FINAL PAYMENT-MR. KNOWLES
